<!-- source: README.md -->

<p align="center"><img src="packaging/desktop/oprobe.svg" width="112" alt="oprobe"></p>

# oprobe

> **oprobe is a profiler for OpenDAL operators.**
> It shows what your `Operator` really does on the wire, names the layer that fixes it, and proves
> the fix before you ship it.

A program has `perf` and flame graphs. An [Apache OpenDAL](https://opendal.apache.org/) operator
has oprobe. It traces every backend request under every operation, stage by stage (queue, connect,
send, time to first byte, body, retry backoff), explains what it finds as **one OpenDAL change**,
and proves that change with an interleaved A/B test on the objective you care about.

[中文](README.zh-CN.md) · [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) · [Concepts](docs/concepts.md) ·
[op.toml](docs/operator.md) · [CLI](docs/cli.md) · [Reading the profile](docs/reading-the-profile.md) ·
[Embedding](docs/embedding.md) · [App](docs/app.md) · [Install](docs/install.md) ·
[Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md)

## The loop: Profile → Explain → Prove

1. **Profile.** Drive a workload through an operator (`oprobe run s3://bucket/prefix`), or open a
   `.oprobe` file that [`oprobe-trace`](docs/embedding.md) wrote in production.
2. **Explain.** Each finding names a cause, shows the requests that are its evidence, and names the
   one OpenDAL remedy. It gives no numbers: a single run varies no load and cannot size a change.
3. **Prove.** `oprobe prove` runs the current operator and the one with the remedy interleaved
   (A B A B …), sizes the remedy where it has a size, and decides on your objective (goodput by
   default, or p99). The result is a **proven layer diff** you can copy.

## Start in 60 seconds

```bash
# install (macOS / Linux; Windows, packages and cargo: docs/install.md)
curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh

oprobe demo                      # profile a misbehaving S3 lab on your laptop: no account needed
oprobe prove last                # A/B-test the remedy of the top finding (about a minute)
oprobe                           # the app: runs, profile, operator, compare
```

`oprobe demo` is `oprobe run lab://demo`: a local S3 that makes every 40th request a straggler
that waits 250 ms (and throttles above 40 requests in flight). The brief names at most three findings,
each with its remedy as an `op.toml` path, and the next command:

```text
[Attention] 2.4% of HeadObject, 2.4% of PutObject and 2.6% of GetObject requests wait far longer for
  the server's first byte than their peers (stragglers).
  lab://demo · small-files · 8.0 s · run 20261123-135409-4b57
  ▲ 1 tail_stragglers (high confidence) — 2.4% of HeadObject, 2.4% of PutObject and 2.6% of
      GetObject requests wait far longer for the server's first byte than their peers (stragglers).
      33 HeadObject stragglers wait ~260ms for the first byte against ~9.48ms for a typical
      HeadObject; 100 PutObject stragglers wait ~260ms for the first byte against ~9.55ms for a
      typical PutObject; 214 GetObject stragglers wait ~260ms for the first byte against ~9.54ms for
      a typical GetObject; operation p50 9.65ms · p99 261ms
      remedy: layers.tail_cut + layers.retry.min_delay — re-issue requests far slower than their
        peers, after a short retry backoff (TailCutLayer + RetryLayer::with_min_delay)
      next: oprobe prove 20261123-135409-4b57 tail_stragglers
  1733.6 ops/s · 97.6 MiB/s · p50 9.65ms · p99 261ms · errors 0.00%
  full profile: oprobe show 20261123-135409-4b57 --detail · terms: https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/blob/v9.3.3/docs/concepts.md#glossary
```

`prove last` runs trials of the current operator (A) and of the remedy (B), interleaved, and ends
with the diff (this run took 54 s):

```text
improved on goodput: +33.3 %, 95 % interval [+26.9, +40.1] (3 pairs of trials, noise ±2.0 %) · lab://demo (local lab)
secondary (not decisive; 95 % intervals): p99 -68.5 % [-70.0, -66.9] · throttled 0.00 % → 0.00 % · errors 0.00 % → 0.00 %
note: TailCutLayer re-issues through RetryLayer: its first backoff is shortened so a cut request is retried at once; trials warm up 11.5 s because the layer ignores its first 10 s
+ TailCutLayer::builder().safety_factor(1.5).min_samples(32).min_deadline(Duration::from_millis(50)).max_deadline(Duration::from_secs(10)).build()
~ RetryLayer::new().with_min_delay(Duration::from_millis(20))
op.toml:
[layers]
retry = { min_delay = "20ms" }
tail_cut = true
```

Then point it at your own storage:

```bash
oprobe run s3://my-bucket/oprobe --set options.region=eu-west-1
oprobe run op.toml --preset range-reads           # your operator, a parquet-like workload
oprobe run s3://a/x r2://b/x fs:///nvme/x         # several operators, one workload: a race
```

Writes go under a fresh `oprobe-run-<id>/` prefix and are cleaned up; `--dry-run` prints the plan,
`--read-only` refuses every write, and `--max-requests/--max-bytes/--max-duration` are hard budgets
(for `prove`, `--max-duration` is the wall-time budget of the whole proof).

## Your operator: `op.toml`

The unit of everything is the OpenDAL `Operator`: a service, a layer stack, and read/write options.
oprobe reads it from a URL or from a file, `op.toml` (the recommended way to describe yours).

```toml
url = "s3://bucket/prefix"
[options]                       # OpenDAL service options
region = "eu-west-1"
[layers]                        # each key is one OpenDAL layer; absent = not in the stack
concurrent_limit = { http = 24 }
retry = { max_times = 3, jitter = true }
timeout = { op = "30s", io = "10s" }
[read]
chunk = "8MiB"
concurrent = 4
[http]
version = "auto"                # auto | h1 | h2
```

`--set layers.retry.max_times=5` or `--set read.gap=1MiB` changes one value. The diff between two
operators renders as Rust and as TOML. [The reference →](docs/operator.md)

## Findings and their remedy

| Finding | Cause | Remedy (`op.toml` path) |
|---|---|---|
| `throttling` | 429/503 above an in-flight level | `layers.concurrent_limit.http`, plus `layers.retry.jitter` |
| `throttling` | a service that queues beyond what it serves at once, with no 429/503 | a cap on the requests in flight, as advice: it moves the wait, there is nothing to prove |
| `rate_limit` | a request-rate ceiling | `layers.concurrent_limit.http` |
| `key_limit` | a hot prefix or key | the key layout (advice, not a layer) |
| `bandwidth_cap` | a bytes-per-second ceiling | `layers.throttle.bandwidth` on a capped uplink (writes); on a capped downlink not a layer |
| `tail_stragglers` | a few very slow server responses | `layers.tail_cut` |
| `hung_requests` | requests that never finish | `layers.timeout.io` |
| `small_ranges` | many small range reads | `read.gap` / `read.concurrent` |
| `slow_multipart` | multipart uploads that crawl | `write.chunk` / `write.concurrent` |
| `repeated_reads` | the same bytes read again and again | `layers.cache` (`FoyerLayer`) |
| `cold_connections` | handshakes on the critical path, HTTP version | `http.keep_alive` / `http.version` |
| `client_bound` | your process is the bottleneck | none in storage; reported as such |
| `errors` | 5xx or lost connections that retries recovered | `layers.retry.min_delay`, plus `layers.retry.jitter` |
| `errors` | writes larger than `layers.throttle.burst`, refused by `ThrottleLayer` | raise `layers.throttle.burst` |
| `errors` | other failures that reached the application | none: fix their cause (`show RUN --by api`) |

`run` names the remedy; only `prove` puts a number on it.

## Profile production: `oprobe-trace`

Add one layer to your own operator and save a profile the workbench opens like any other run:

```toml
[dependencies]
oprobe-trace = { git = "https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe", tag = "v9.3.3" }   # not on crates.io yet
```

```rust
let (layer, handle) = oprobe_trace::layer(oprobe_trace::Config::default());
let op = op.layer(layer);
handle.save("prod.oprobe")?;          // later: oprobe show prod.oprobe
```

`oprobe-trace` is an OpenDAL layer plus an instrumented `HttpFetch` (OpenDAL's own reqwest client,
observed). Memory stays bounded, the overhead is benchmarked (budget ≤ 2 µs per operation), and an
`Exporter` hook (with OpenTelemetry metrics behind the `otel` feature) sees every request.
[Embedding →](docs/embedding.md)

## The app

Run `oprobe` with no arguments: a native window when there is a display, the same app in your
terminal otherwise (also over SSH). Four views: **Runs**, **Profile** (verdict, where the time
went, the request waterfall of the slowest operations, timeline, heatmap), **Operator** (your layer
stack beside each remedy: toggle a layer, press *Prove*, watch the trials stream in, copy the
diff) and **Compare**. It speaks 简体中文 and English. [More →](docs/app.md)

## For scripts and agents

Every command prints one JSON document with `-o json` (stdout carries only the result; progress
goes to stderr), errors carry stable codes and exit codes (0 ok · 1 runtime · 2 usage · 3 prove: worse
· 4 budget · 5 safety · 130 interrupted), and the JSON Schemas are in [`schemas/`](schemas).
Agents: [`skills/oprobe/SKILL.md`](skills/oprobe/SKILL.md) and [llms.txt](llms.txt).

Two patterns cover CI:

```sh
# Fail the job when a profile is critical.
oprobe run s3://bucket/bench --existing data/ --max-requests 20000 -o json \
  | jq -e '.runs[0].report.verdict.level != "critical"'
# Fail the job when a change makes the operator worse: prove exits 3.
oprobe prove last --with layers.retry.max_times=5 --max-duration 5m -o json > prove.json
```

## Install

| Platform | |
|---|---|
| macOS / Linux | `curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh \| sh` (`-s -- --cli` for the CLI without the app) |
| Windows | `irm https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 \| iex` or the `.msi` |
| Debian / Ubuntu, Fedora / RHEL | `.deb` / `.rpm` from the release page |
| Rust (from source) | `cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe --tag v9.3.3 oprobe` (`--no-default-features --features cli` for the CLI only, `--features gui` for native windows on Linux) |

The macOS and Windows packages are **not code-signed**: the first open needs one confirmation
([how](docs/install.md#first-open-of-unsigned-packages)). Every asset has a SHA-256 in `SHA256SUMS`
and a SLSA build provenance attestation; the install scripts check the SHA-256 and, when the GitHub
CLI is logged in, the attestation ([verifying](docs/install.md#verifying-a-download)).

oprobe sends no telemetry and talks only to the storage you point it at. [Privacy →](docs/privacy.md)

<!-- source: docs/getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

Ten minutes from install to a proven change: profile the local lab, explain what it finds, prove
the fix, then do the same on your own storage. No account is needed until the last step.

## 1. Install

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
# Windows, packages, from source: docs/install.md
```

## 2. Profile the lab

```bash
oprobe demo
```

`demo` is `oprobe run lab://demo`. The lab is an S3-compatible server inside oprobe on 127.0.0.1:
every 40th request is a straggler that waits 250 ms for its first byte, and it throttles
(503 SlowDown) above 40 requests in flight. The default workload writes, reads and stats small objects
with 16 workers for 8 seconds:

```text
[Attention] 2.4% of HeadObject, 2.4% of PutObject and 2.6% of GetObject requests wait far longer for
  the server's first byte than their peers (stragglers).
  lab://demo · small-files · 8.0 s · run 20261123-135409-4b57
  ▲ 1 tail_stragglers (high confidence) — 2.4% of HeadObject, 2.4% of PutObject and 2.6% of
      GetObject requests wait far longer for the server's first byte than their peers (stragglers).
      33 HeadObject stragglers wait ~260ms for the first byte against ~9.48ms for a typical
      HeadObject; 100 PutObject stragglers wait ~260ms for the first byte against ~9.55ms for a
      typical PutObject; 214 GetObject stragglers wait ~260ms for the first byte against ~9.54ms for
      a typical GetObject; operation p50 9.65ms · p99 261ms
      remedy: layers.tail_cut + layers.retry.min_delay — re-issue requests far slower than their
        peers, after a short retry backoff (TailCutLayer + RetryLayer::with_min_delay)
      next: oprobe prove 20261123-135409-4b57 tail_stragglers
  1733.6 ops/s · 97.6 MiB/s · p50 9.65ms · p99 261ms · errors 0.00%
  full profile: oprobe show 20261123-135409-4b57 --detail · terms: https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/blob/v7.0.0/docs/concepts.md#glossary
```

The brief that `run` prints has three parts:

- **the verdict**: its level (OK, Review, Attention, Critical) and the top finding's cause;
- **at most three findings**, costliest first, each with its cause, its evidence (counts and the
  requests themselves) and its remedy as an `op.toml` path, such as `layers.tail_cut`;
- **the next command**, `oprobe prove RUN FINDING`.

Here every API has stragglers: each holds a worker for a quarter of a second, so the slowest 2.5 %
of requests cost the run a third of its throughput.

The run is saved. `oprobe show last` prints the whole profile, `oprobe show last --by stage`
groups the requests by stage, and `oprobe show --list` lists the history.

## 3. Prove the remedy

```bash
oprobe prove last
```

`prove` takes the run's operator (A) and the same operator with the top finding's remedy (B);
`oprobe prove last FINDING` proves another finding's. For a remedy with a size, such as a
concurrency limit, it first runs short sizing trials over that one value and picks the knee of
the objective. Then it runs trials of A and B interleaved, pair by pair in a balanced order,
until a sequential test against the noise floor decides, or the budget (`--max-duration`) runs
out. It starts with the
number of trials and the ETA of the whole proof, and prints each trial as it ends (on stderr):

```text
prove tail_stragglers · goodput · run 20261123-135409-4b57 · prove 20261123-135419-219a
6–12 trials (3–6 pairs of A and B) · ETA 57s – 1m 53s
· A #1 : 1757.9 ops/s · p99 261ms · 0.00 % throttled
· B #1 : 2354.5 ops/s · p99 82.2ms · 0.00 % throttled
· A #2 : 1747.9 ops/s · p99 261ms · 0.00 % throttled
· B #2 : 2330.5 ops/s · p99 82.2ms · 0.00 % throttled
· A #3 : 1765.4 ops/s · p99 261ms · 0.00 % throttled
· B #3 : 2343.0 ops/s · p99 82.1ms · 0.00 % throttled
```

The verdict is `improved`, `worse` (exit 3) or `inconclusive`, on goodput unless you pass
`--objective p99`, and the result ends with the diff:

```text
improved on goodput: +33.3 %, 95 % interval [+26.9, +40.1] (3 pairs of trials, noise ±2.0 %) · lab://demo (local lab)
secondary (not decisive; 95 % intervals): p99 -68.5 % [-70.0, -66.9] · throttled 0.00 % → 0.00 % · errors 0.00 % → 0.00 %
note: TailCutLayer re-issues through RetryLayer: its first backoff is shortened so a cut request is retried at once; trials warm up 11.5 s because the layer ignores its first 10 s
+ TailCutLayer::builder().safety_factor(1.5).min_samples(32).min_deadline(Duration::from_millis(50)).max_deadline(Duration::from_secs(10)).build()
~ RetryLayer::new().with_min_delay(Duration::from_millis(20))
op.toml:
[layers]
retry = { min_delay = "20ms" }
tail_cut = true
```

The diff is Rust you can paste into your operator, and the same change as `op.toml`. TailCutLayer
ignores its first 10 seconds, so its candidate trials warm up for 11.5 s: this proof took a
minute. To prove a change of your own: `oprobe prove last --with layers.retry.jitter=on`.

## 4. Open the app

```bash
oprobe
```

The app shows the same runs in a sidebar. A run opens in Profile or Operator, and two or more selected runs open in Compare. In the Operator
view you can toggle a layer, press *Prove* and watch the trials arrive. See [the app](app.md).

## 5. Your storage

oprobe uses the credentials your OpenDAL code would use (`AWS_*`, `~/.aws` profiles,
`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, `AZURE_STORAGE_*`), or the options in `op.toml`.

```bash
oprobe run s3://my-bucket/oprobe --dry-run      # the plan: requests, bytes, objects, ETA
oprobe run s3://my-bucket/oprobe --set options.region=eu-west-1
```

Writes go under `s3://my-bucket/oprobe/oprobe-run-<id>/` and are deleted at the end. To touch
nothing, profile existing objects read-only: `--existing data/2026/`. Budgets stop a run hard:
`--max-requests 100000 --max-bytes 10GiB --max-duration 5m`.

Put your real operator in a file and profile it on the workload that looks like yours:

```bash
cat > op.toml <<'EOF'
url = "s3://my-bucket/oprobe"
[options]
region = "eu-west-1"
[layers]
retry = { max_times = 4, jitter = true }
[read]
chunk = "8MiB"
concurrent = 4
EOF
oprobe run op.toml --preset range-reads
```

The four presets are `small-files`, `large-objects`, `range-reads` and `list-stat`
([concepts](concepts.md#workload)). Several operators run one after another on the same workload
and form one comparison: `oprobe run op.toml 'r2://bucket/x?account_id=ACCOUNT_ID'` (R2 needs the Cloudflare account id, or an endpoint).

## 6. Production

To profile the traffic your service already sends, add the [`oprobe-trace`](embedding.md) layer
to its operator and open the `.oprobe` file it saves with `oprobe show FILE` or in the app.

Next: [concepts](concepts.md) · [op.toml](operator.md) · [reading the profile](reading-the-profile.md)
· [CLI](cli.md)


<!-- source: docs/concepts.md -->

# Concepts

oprobe has six ideas: the **operator** you profile, the **workload** you drive through it, the
**profile** that comes out, the **findings** in it, each finding's **remedy**, and **prove**, which
turns a remedy into a number.

## Operator

An OpenDAL `Operator` is a service (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, a file system, …), a stack of layers
(retry, timeout, concurrency limit, …) and the options of its reads and writes. That is OpenDAL's
own model, and it is the unit of everything in oprobe.

oprobe reads an operator from:

- a URL: `s3://bucket/prefix`, `gcs://bucket`, `azblob://container`, `fs:///nvme/x`, `memory://`,
  or `lab://SCENARIO` for the built-in lab; the layers are OpenDAL's defaults plus `retry` and
  `timeout`;
- an operator file, `op.toml` (format `oprobe.operator/6`): the URL, service options, layers,
  read/write options and HTTP client settings ([reference](operator.md));
- a name, `[operators.NAME]` in the config file (an `op.toml` path is the recommended way;
  [the config file](operator.md#the-config-file)).

`--set PATH=VALUE` changes one value (`--set layers.retry.max_times=5`, `--set read.gap=1MiB`).
The difference between two operators is itself a value: it renders as Rust builder code and as
TOML, and it is what `prove` hands you.

Comparing two operators that differ in a layer is the same thing as comparing two that differ in
service. So `oprobe run s3://a/x r2://b/x fs:///nvme/x` races three backends with no extra
feature.

## Workload

A workload is an OpenDAL access pattern. Four presets cover the common ones:

| Preset | What it does | Default dataset |
|---|---|---|
| `small-files` (default) | whole-object reads (60 %) and writes (30 %), stats (10 %) | 256 × 64 KiB |
| `large-objects` | multipart writes (80 %) and full reads (20 %) | 2 × 32 MiB |
| `range-reads` | parquet-like: a stat, the footer, then vectored column-chunk ranges | 8 × 16 MiB |
| `list-stat` | lists (40 %) and stats (60 %) over a partitioned prefix | 512 × 4 KiB in 16 partitions |

Shape it with `-c/--concurrency`, `-d/--duration`, `--objects`, `--object-size`, `--rate`
(open loop: operations start on a schedule and latency counts from the intended start, so a slow
server cannot hide behind fewer requests), `--seed` and `--existing PREFIX` (read the objects
that are already there, write nothing).

oprobe writes its dataset under a fresh `oprobe-run-<id>/` prefix, warms up, measures, and
deletes the prefix. A run killed before it could clean up leaves its prefix behind; the next run
against the same target deletes it. The guard enforces budgets (`--max-requests`, `--max-bytes`,
`--max-duration`), `--read-only` and `--dry-run`.

**Budgets hold on the wire.** `--max-requests` and `--max-bytes` count every HTTP request the
command sends to the target and every body byte, as they are sent and received:

- in every phase before cleanup: the reachability check, the preflight, the dataset upload, the
  warm-up, the measurement and the verification of written objects;
- retries and re-sent requests included, each with its body;
- a request the budget has no room for is never sent, and a download stops at the chunk that
  crosses the byte budget, so a budget is overshot by at most the response chunks in flight,
  never by a whole operation;
- once a budget is spent, nothing more is sent: a request without a body is refused too, since
  its answer would only be cut. A body that does not fit in what is left of `--max-bytes` is
  refused and the error says so ("the next request (8.0 MiB) does not fit the byte budget: 1 B
  of 4.0 MiB used");
- cleanup is never counted and never refused: deleting the run prefix, deleting the preflight's
  probe object and aborting multipart uploads always run.

In-process services (`memory://`, `fs://`) send no HTTP request: their calls are counted as they
complete.

**A stopped run leaves no multipart upload.** When a budget, `--max-duration`, Ctrl-C (or
SIGTERM, SIGHUP), a closed terminal or Stop ends a run, the requests in flight are cut and the
operations they belong to end at once; they are neither completed nor failed operations, and are
not in the profile (an open-loop run counts them in neither its arrivals nor its achieved rate).
Every multipart upload a failed, timed-out or stopped write or dataset upload had started is
aborted (`AbortMultipartUpload`), so no part stays on the target to be billed where no object
listing shows it.

Stopping is bounded. An upload that was being created when the run stopped has 10 s to answer
(its answer carries the id it is aborted with), each abort 30 s, and the run waits at most 45 s
for all of them before it deletes its test data. An upload whose abort failed, whose creation
never answered or that was still in flight after that wait is named in the cleanup error: check
the target for it (`aws s3api list-multipart-uploads`, or a lifecycle rule that aborts
incomplete uploads).

**A closed stderr stops the run like a signal.** Progress goes to stderr. When its reader is
gone (the terminal or SSH session closed, `oprobe run … 2>&1 | head`), the first line that cannot
be written stops the command as Ctrl-C does: it cleans up, saves the partial run and exits 130.
With `-q` nothing is written while the run measures, so it runs to its end.

## Profile

A profile is what one operator did on one workload, saved as one `.oprobe` file:

- the operator spec and the workload, so the run can be reproduced exactly;
- every operation and every backend request under it, stage by stage: **queue** (waiting for a
  connection or a permit), **connect** (DNS, TCP, proxy, TLS on a fresh connection), **send**,
  **TTFB** (the server's time to the first byte), **body** (the transfer), **stall** (the body
  waiting for your code), and **retry backoff** between attempts;
- the aggregates: throughput and goodput, latency percentiles, per API and per stage, connection
  reuse, bytes and amplification, a per-second timeline and a latency heatmap;
- the findings.

Each operation's wall time splits exactly into queue + backend + retry + client, so "network,
server or my code?" has a measured answer. Long runs keep every aggregate exact and sample whole
operations (failed, throttled and slowest ones first: a run that fails for hours thins those
too), so memory and the run file stay bounded.

`.oprobe` files come from `oprobe run` and from [`oprobe-trace`](embedding.md) in production;
`oprobe show FILE` and the app open both. A production trace has the same shape: every OpenDAL
call your application makes is an operation with its requests, its keys hashed. What it lacks is
a workload oprobe chose, so nothing to replay: `prove` needs a run. [Reading the profile
→](reading-the-profile.md)

## Finding

A finding names a cause and shows its evidence. It is derived from the profile by fitting simple
limit models to the requests in flight over time (an in-flight ceiling where 429/503 start, or
where the service starts to queue requests without rejecting any; a request-rate ceiling; a
bandwidth plateau of the downloads or of the uploads; a hot key) and by reading the stage split (stragglers,
hung I/O, cold connections, small ranges, slow multipart, repeated reads, a busy client).

Every finding has a confidence: **high** only when the model explains most of the effect and
agrees across repeats. Throttling that made operations fail is reported as throttling, never as
an invalid run, and a handful of 429/503 that no limit model explains is still `throttling`, at
low confidence, never `errors`. The codes and their remedies are in the
[README](../README.md#findings-and-their-remedy); besides those, `errors` reports failures that
are not throttling and `invalid_run` a run whose numbers cannot be trusted (too short, nothing
measured). The remedy of `errors` follows what failed:

- transient failures the retries recovered (5xx, lost connections), a few operations that ran
  out of retries included: a shorter first retry backoff with jitter (`layers.retry.min_delay`);
- writes that OpenDAL's `ThrottleLayer` refused because they are larger than
  `layers.throttle.burst` (they fail as rate-limited with no 429/503 from the service): raise
  the burst to at least the largest write;
- anything else (credentials, permissions, the endpoint): not a layer.

## Remedy

Each finding names exactly **one** remedy, as an `op.toml` path: `layers.concurrent_limit.http`,
`layers.tail_cut`, `read.gap`, `http.keep_alive`, … A remedy that is not a layer (spreading keys
over prefixes for `key_limit`), or that no A/B test can measure (capping the requests in flight
in front of a service that queues without rejecting: the cap moves the wait, it shortens
nothing), is reported as advice, and `client_bound` has no storage remedy: their `next` says
where to look (`oprobe show RUN --detail`), and `prove` refuses them.

`run` gives the remedy and **no number**. A single run varies no load, so it cannot say how
large a limit should be or how much it would help; claiming so would be a guess.

## Prove

`oprobe prove RUN [FINDING]` is the only source of numbers:

1. **Choose the change**: the finding's remedy (the top finding by default), or `--with PATH=VALUE`.
2. **Size it**: when the remedy has a size (a limit, a chunk), short trials over that one value
   find the knee of the objective, within `--max-throttle`. For a `rate_limit` finding the
   value must also stay under the rate the finding fitted: a cap whose own trial sends more
   requests per second than that is not chosen, even when its two seconds saw no throttle (a
   token bucket's burst hides the limit from a short trial).
3. **A/B test**: trials of A and B run in pairs. The order is balanced: the pairs come in blocks
   of two, one `AB` and one `BA`, and which comes first in a block is drawn from the run's seed.
   A sequential test on the objective, against a noise floor learned from each side's
   consecutive trials (the A/A spread until B has its own), stops as soon as it can decide, or
   when the wall-time budget (`--max-duration`) would be exceeded. A trial that ends throttled
   is followed by a short cool-down, so the next trial (often the other side) does not start
   against a limit the last one drained.
4. **Decide**: `improved`, `worse` (exit 3) or `inconclusive` on the objective: **goodput**
   (successful operations per second; the default) or **p99**. The verdict is whether the
   objective's interval excludes no change, and nothing else:
   - The estimate is the mean of the paired log ratios (B over A, pair by pair), taken as the
     mean of the `AB` pairs' mean and the `BA` pairs' mean. An effect of the order itself (the
     second trial of a pair running warmer, or against a refilled limit) cancels in it.
   - The spread is the larger of the pairs' own spread and the A/A noise floor. The interval
     never goes below −100 %.
   - The interval is **sequential**: prove looks after every pair from the third on, so each
     look is held to a stricter level than one fixed-size test would be (the critical values
     are calibrated by simulation for the planned number of pairs, `--pairs`). Whenever the
     proof stops — a decision, the pair limit, the budget — the chance that it calls a change
     that is none stays under 5 %. An order effect widens the interval; it never moves it.
   - The proof also stops early when more pairs would not help (**futility**): the pairs so
     far rule out the smallest change the planned pairs could show at the noise measured. A
     note names that smallest change. A proof is never given up for a change it could have
     shown.
   - **After an early stop, read the interval, not the estimate.** A proof that stops early
     on a decision stopped because its estimate was large, so the estimate overstates the
     change on average. The interval does not: its coverage holds whenever the proof stops.
   - Shares (throttled requests, errors) are compared with Newcombe's interval. Secondary
     metrics are shown and never decide; each has a plain interval (not sequential) on its
     own trial-to-trial spread, not the objective's.
   - Deciding takes at least 3 pairs of trials; with fewer, the verdict is `inconclusive`.
   - **Two gates come before the objective.** A changed operator that throttles more than
     `--max-throttle` allows, or fails more operations than the run allows (1 %), and more
     than the current operator beyond chance, is `inconclusive` with a note: operations that
     fail fast lower a p99, and that is no improvement. A pair in which a trial has no
     objective at all (no successful operation, nothing measured) is not judged, and ends
     the proof.
   - **A p99 needs enough operations.** The p99 of a trial is one order statistic: its
     resolution is the spread of the latencies at the ranks 0.99·n ± 2·√(0.0099·n) of the
     trial's n operations, and the noise floor is never below it. When those latencies
     differ by more than 2× the p99 sits on a cliff (the edge of the throttled or retried
     operations, say), which side a trial lands on is chance, and a note says "p99 sits on a
     cliff: lengthen the trial" (`--trial`).
5. **Save**: every trial is saved as a run, a child of the prove, hidden from `show --list`.

The result is a **proven layer diff**: the objective's change with its interval, the evidence,
and the change as Rust and as TOML. Every result states where it was validated (the lab, MinIO,
your bucket).

## Glossary

The terms a profile and a proof print, in one line each.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **operation** | one OpenDAL call (`read`, `write`, `stat`, `list`, …); it may send several requests |
| **request** | one HTTP request to the service; retries and range parts are requests of one operation |
| **throughput** | operations (or MiB) per second, failed ones included |
| **goodput** | *successful* operations per second: the work that got done; `prove`'s default objective |
| **p50 / p99** | the latency half / 99 % of operations stay under; p99 is the slowest 1 % |
| **TTFB** | time to first byte: from the request sent to the first byte of the answer (the server's time, plus one network round trip) |
| **queue · connect · send · body · stall** | the stages of a request: waiting for a connection or a permit, opening one (DNS, TCP, TLS), sending, receiving the body, and the body waiting for your code |
| **retry backoff** | time an operation sleeps between attempts after a 429, 503 or another retryable failure |
| **throttled** | answered 429 (Too Many Requests) or 503 (Slow Down): the service refuses load; `throttled %` is the share of requests |
| **in flight** | requests sent and not yet answered at one moment; a limit "starts above N in flight" |
| **stragglers** | the few requests far slower than a typical one, usually waiting on the server (TTFB) |
| **amplification** | bytes or requests per operation above what the operation needed (over-read ranges, retries) |
| **cold connection** | a request that had to open a new connection instead of reusing one |
| **open loop** | operations start on a schedule (`--rate`), so a slow service cannot hide behind fewer requests |
| **confidence** | how well a finding's model explains the evidence: high, medium or low |
| **95 % interval** | the range `[low, high]` that holds the true change in 95 of 100 repeats of the proof, whenever the proof stopped (it is sequential, and adjusted for the order of the trials in a pair); a change whose interval includes 0 is not proven |
| **noise floor (`±`)** | how much two runs of the *same* operator differ (the A/A spread); a change smaller than it cannot be told from noise |
| **pair of trials** | one short run of A (the operator as it is) and one of B (with the change), back to back |
| **verdict** | `ok`, `review` (look before trusting the numbers), `attention` (a finding costs time) or `critical` (failures or a large cost) |

## Where oprobe stops

oprobe is not a load generator for benchmarking storage servers (use warp or elbencho), not a
monitoring system (use OpenDAL's metrics and OpenTelemetry layers, or `oprobe-trace`'s
exporter), not a CI regression gate and not a cloud bill estimator.


<!-- source: docs/operator.md -->

# The operator file: `op.toml`

An operator file describes one OpenDAL `Operator`: the service, its layer stack, the options of
its reads and writes, and its HTTP client. Its format is `oprobe.operator/6` (JSON Schema:
[`schemas/operator.json`](../schemas/operator.json)). The same value builds the operator oprobe
measures, is what `--set` changes, and renders the difference between two operators as Rust and
TOML.

```toml
url = "s3://bucket/prefix"          # any OpenDAL scheme oprobe is built with; lab:// too
[options]                            # OpenDAL service options, checked against the service
region = "eu-west-1"
[layers]                             # each key = one OpenDAL layer; absent = its default
concurrent_limit = { http = 24 }                    # ConcurrentLimitLayer
retry = { max_times = 3, jitter = true, min_delay = "50ms", max_delay = "5s" }   # RetryLayer
timeout = { op = "30s", io = "10s" }                # TimeoutLayer
tail_cut = { percentile = 95 }                      # TailCutLayer
throttle = { bandwidth = "100MiB", burst = "16MiB" }  # ThrottleLayer
cache = { memory = "256MiB" }                       # FoyerLayer (in-memory)
[read]
chunk = "8MiB"
concurrent = 4
gap = "64KiB"
[write]
chunk = "8MiB"
concurrent = 4
[http]
version = "auto"          # auto | h1 | h2
keep_alive = true
```

Unknown keys are errors. Sizes are `"64KiB"`, `"8MiB"`, `"1GB"` or a number of bytes; durations
are `"50ms"`, `"10s"`, `"5m"`.

## `url`

The service: `s3://bucket/prefix`, `gcs://bucket/prefix`, `azblob://container/prefix`,
`oss://…`, `cos://…`, `obs://…`, `b2://…`, `webdav://…`, `fs:///path`, `memory://`, or
`lab://SCENARIO` for the built-in lab. Release builds include S3, GCS, Azure Blob, OSS, COS, OBS,
B2 and WebDAV;
`cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe oprobe --features all-services`
adds the rest OpenDAL offers to oprobe (Azure Data Lake, Azure Files, Swift, TOS, WebHDFS, UpYun, HTTP).

## `[options]`

OpenDAL service options, by their OpenDAL names: `region`, `endpoint`, `access_key_id`,
`enable_virtual_host_style`, `account_name`, `credential_path`, … An option the service does not
know is an error that names the closest valid one (`config.unknown_option`). Values may reference
environment variables as `${NAME}`. Credential options are redacted before anything is printed or
saved.

## `[layers]`

Each key is one OpenDAL layer. The defaults are OpenDAL's, plus `retry` and `timeout`, which
OpenDAL recommends:

- a key that is absent keeps its default: **on** for `retry` and `timeout`, **off** for the rest;
- `false` (or `--set layers.NAME=off`) takes the layer out of the stack;
- `true` (or `--set layers.NAME=on`) puts it in with its default parameters;
- a table puts it in with those parameters.

| Key | OpenDAL layer | Fields (default) |
|---|---|---|
| `concurrent_limit` | `ConcurrentLimitLayer` | `http`: HTTP requests in flight (`with_http_concurrent_limit`); `operations`: operations in flight (`ConcurrentLimitLayer::new`; unset: unlimited) |
| `retry` | `RetryLayer` | `max_times` (3), `jitter` (false), `min_delay` ("1s"), `max_delay` ("60s"), `factor` (2.0) |
| `timeout` | `TimeoutLayer` | `op`: one operation ("60s"); `io`: one read or write call ("10s") |
| `tail_cut` | `TailCutLayer` | cancel and re-issue requests slower than `percentile` (95, within 50..99) of the recent latencies × `safety_factor` (1.5, within 1..5), once `min_samples` (32) latencies are recorded within `window` ("60s", at most 120 s); the deadline is clamped to `min_deadline` ("50ms") .. `max_deadline` (unset: the shorter of `layers.timeout.op` and `layers.timeout.io`, the timeouts that sever the same calls, so the ceiling is one the layer can reach; 60 s without the timeout layer). These defaults are oprobe's, not OpenDAL's (1.3, 200, "500ms", "30s"); generated Rust spells out every value that differs from OpenDAL's, so pasted code behaves as measured |
| `throttle` | `ThrottleLayer` | `bandwidth` ("100MiB" per second), `burst` ("16MiB") |
| `cache` | `FoyerLayer` over an in-memory foyer cache, each entry weighed by its size | `memory` ("256MiB" of cached data): any object no larger than `memory` is cached whole; a larger one is read through |

### The order of the stack

The layers are stacked in one fixed order, whatever the order of the keys. A call passes them
from the outside in:

```text
cache → retry → throttle → concurrent_limit → tail_cut → timeout → service
```

The operator oprobe measures and the Rust it generates are both built from this one list, so
pasted code stacks the layers exactly as they were measured.

- **`timeout` and `tail_cut` time one call to the service and nothing else.** `tail_cut` is the
  outer of the two; its default ceiling is the shorter of the two timeouts, because OpenDAL's
  `TimeoutLayer` gives `stat`-like calls `op` and every read, write, list and delete call `io`.
- **Waiting for an operation permit is not timed.** `concurrent_limit` is outside both timers: a
  call that queues for `operations` neither runs into a timeout nor counts as a slow call that
  `tail_cut` would cut and re-issue into the same queue.
- **A throttled write waits before it takes a permit.** `throttle` is outside the limiter and the
  timers, so its wait is neither a held permit nor a slow call.
- **A write larger than `throttle.burst` fails; it does not wait.** `ThrottleLayer` refuses a
  single write above the burst with `rate_limited` ("burst size is smaller than the request
  size"). Keep `burst` at least as large as the largest single write: `write.chunk` when it is
  set (oprobe refuses a `burst` below it), otherwise the largest buffer the application writes
  at once, which for a workload without `write.chunk` can be a whole object.
- **Every attempt starts over.** `retry` is outside all of them: a retried call is throttled,
  limited and timed again, and a `stat` or a read gives its permit back during the backoff.
- **A cache hit touches nothing else.**

Two things OpenDAL's design leaves as they are:

- The HTTP permit of `concurrent_limit.http` is taken inside the service, where OpenDAL wraps
  the HTTP transport. Waiting for it is therefore always inside `timeout` and `tail_cut`: a
  request that queues behind a small `http` limit can time out, or be tail-cut, while it queues.
  The profile shows that wait as queue time.
- A writer, a lister and a deleter keep their operation permit from their first call until
  they are dropped, a retry's backoff included. So only the first write of an upload waits for
  the throttle without a permit; its later parts are throttled while the writer holds it.

### The cache

`cache = { memory = "256MiB" }` is one byte budget. The foyer cache behind it has a single
shard, weighs each entry by its object's size and admits any object no larger than `memory`;
`FoyerLayer` gets the same size limit, so a larger object is read through with ordinary ranged
requests and is never fetched or buffered whole. (Foyer's default of 8 shards splits the budget
by key hash: an object above an eighth of it could not be cached, and a budget that covers the
objects read still evicted whenever one shard filled first.) The generated Rust builds the
same cache: `.with_shards(1)`, the weighter, and `.with_size_limit(..=memory)`.

What `FoyerLayer` costs, as OpenDAL 0.59 implements it:

- **A ranged read caches the whole object.** The first read of an object, of any range, fetches
  the object whole and keeps it; later reads are slices of it. A cache therefore pays off for
  objects that are read again, and costs more than it saves for a few small ranges of large
  objects.
- **A `HEAD` before every read that misses.** The layer asks for the object's size first. An
  object larger than `memory` is then read through, and the next read of it asks again: one
  extra `HEAD` per read of an oversize object.
- **A write is buffered until it is closed.** A write through the layer is also kept in memory,
  up to `memory`, and enters the cache when the writer closes. A writer of a larger object
  stops buffering once it passes `memory`.
- **Nothing expires.** An entry stays until the budget evicts it. An object that another client
  changes or deletes is served from the cache as it was.

`prove` sizes `memory` from the distinct objects the run read, with a quarter of headroom, up to
1 GiB. It sizes no cache at all, and says why, when the largest object read is above 1 GiB, or
when the reads are ranges of objects that hold more bytes than the run read of them: the layer
would fetch more than it could save. `--with layers.cache.memory=SIZE` still tests any cache.

**Known issue (OpenDAL 0.59, versioned buckets): a stale read after a write.** The layer keys a
written object by the version the service returns for the write, and an ordinary read by no
version. On a bucket with versioning on, an object that was read, then overwritten through the
same operator, is still served as it was before the write, until the old entry is evicted. On a
bucket without versioning the write replaces the entry. Do not put `cache` on an operator that
overwrites objects it also reads in a versioned bucket.

## `[read]` and `[write]`

The options of `read_with` / `reader_with` and `writer_with`; unset means OpenDAL's default.

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `read.chunk` | read in chunks of this size |
| `read.concurrent` | chunks fetched at once |
| `read.gap` | merge ranges closer than this into one request |
| `write.chunk` | multipart part size (OpenDAL clamps it to the service's limits; the profile shows the effective value). Unset, OpenDAL fixes no part size: it buffers up to the service's minimum and sends each write as it comes, so the parts are as large as the caller's writes, and the profile shows the parts that were uploaded |
| `write.concurrent` | parts uploaded at once |

## `[http]`

OpenDAL's HTTP transport (`ReqwestTransport`, installed with
`OperationContext::new().with_http_transport(HttpTransporter::new(ReqwestTransport::new(client)))`).

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `version` | `auto` (OpenDAL's default: HTTP/1.1), `h1` or `h2` |
| `keep_alive` | reuse connections (default true) |
| `proxy` | egress proxy URL; `"none"` (also `--set http.proxy=none`) means no proxy, whatever `HTTPS_PROXY`/`HTTP_PROXY` say; unset (`--set http.proxy=unset`): the environment |
| `ca_cert` | an extra PEM CA bundle to trust (relative paths in `op.toml` resolve against the file's directory) |
| `insecure` | skip certificate verification (self-signed development endpoints only) |

## `--set`

`--set PATH=VALUE` (repeatable) changes one value of the operator before a run; `prove --with`
takes the same paths. The paths: `url`, `options.KEY`, `layers.NAME` (`on`/`off`),
`layers.NAME.FIELD`, `read.chunk`, `read.concurrent`, `read.gap`, `write.chunk`,
`write.concurrent`, `http.version`, `http.keep_alive`, `http.proxy`, `http.ca_cert`,
`http.insecure`. `none` removes an optional value, except for `http.proxy`, where it means no proxy
(`unset` goes back to the environment's).

`--set` also takes the workload's keys, the ones without a flag of their own included:
`concurrency`, `preset`, `duration`, `warmup` (e.g. `--set warmup=2s`), `max_ops`, `rate`,
`arrivals`, `shape`, `access`, `objects`, `object_size`, `partitions`, `existing`, `persist`,
`verify`, `cleanup`, `seed` and `mix`; and the run's `label`. There are no limits to set: the
findings judge a run, an open loop that stalled fails its checks by itself (see
[reading the profile](reading-the-profile.md#how-it-is-measured)), and `prove --max-throttle`
bounds the throttling a sized change may cause.

```bash
oprobe run op.toml --set layers.concurrent_limit.http=32 --set read.gap=1MiB
oprobe run s3://bucket/bench -d 10s --set warmup=1s
oprobe prove last --with layers.retry.jitter=true
```

## The config file

`$OPROBE_CONFIG`, or `<config dir>/oprobe/config.toml` (`~/.config/oprobe/config.toml` on Linux,
`~/Library/Application Support/oprobe/config.toml` on macOS, `%APPDATA%\oprobe\config.toml` on
Windows). It sets defaults:

```toml
[defaults]
preset = "range-reads"
duration = "30s"

[defaults.budgets]
max_requests = 200000
max_bytes = "20GiB"
```

Precedence of every setting: flags, then `OPROBE_*` environment variables, then `[defaults]`,
then the built-in default.

**Your operator belongs in an `op.toml` file**, passed by its path: `oprobe run prod.toml`. It
can live next to your code, be reviewed and versioned, and is what `prove`'s TOML diff patches.
The config file can also name an operator, as a shortcut for the same table:

```toml
[operators.prod]
url = "s3://prod-bucket/oprobe"
[operators.prod.options]
region = "eu-west-1"
[operators.prod.layers]
concurrent_limit = { http = 64 }
```

`oprobe run prod` then profiles that operator.

## The diff

`prove` and the app's Operator view show the difference between two operators as Rust builder
code and as TOML:

```text
+ ConcurrentLimitLayer::new(1 << 20).with_http_concurrent_limit(24)
~ RetryLayer::new().with_jitter().with_max_times(4)

[layers]
concurrent_limit = { http = 24 }
retry = { max_times = 4, jitter = true }
```

`+` adds a layer, `~` changes one, `-` removes one. The lines are in the order of the stack,
innermost first, and each expression is the one oprobe built the measured layer from.

Secrets are never part of the code. A credential option given as a value shows as
`"<redacted>"` in the TOML and, in the Rust, as a line that names the option without a value:
nothing to paste over the credential your program loads itself. An option given as an
environment reference (`secret_access_key = "${MY_SECRET}"`) is kept as the reference in the
TOML and read with `std::env::var("MY_SECRET")?` in the Rust.


<!-- source: docs/cli.md -->

# CLI reference

oprobe has four commands and an alias. Without a command it opens [the app](app.md).

```text
oprobe                     # the app (a native window, or the terminal without a display)
oprobe run   OPERATOR…     # profile; several operators = side by side
oprobe demo                # = oprobe run lab://demo
oprobe prove RUN [FINDING] # A/B test → the proven layer diff
oprobe show  [RUN|FILE]…   # the profile (several = side by side); --list for history
oprobe lab   [SCENARIO]    # a local S3 with faults
```

`oprobe COMMAND --help` prints the same flags as this page; a test keeps the two in sync.

## Global flags

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-o, --output text\|json` | the result on stdout as text (default) or one JSON document (env `OPROBE_OUTPUT`); logs and progress always go to stderr |
| `--color auto\|always\|never` | colors (default `auto`; `NO_COLOR` is honoured) |
| `-q, --quiet` | no progress or informational messages on stderr |
| `--non-interactive` | never prompt or redraw (implied when stdin or stdout is not a terminal) |
| `-h, --help` | help (`-h` for a summary) |
| `-V, --version` | the version |

## `oprobe run OPERATOR…`

Profile one or more operators on the same workload. Several operators run one after another on
the same workload and form one comparison. Prints the brief: the verdict, at most three findings
with their remedy, and the next command. The run is saved; `-o json` prints the runs, each
with its report, and the comparison when there are several (`schemas/run.json`; the report alone
is `schemas/report.json`).

`OPERATOR` is a URL (`s3://bucket/prefix`, `lab://demo`, `fs:///tmp/x`, `memory://`) or an
operator file ([`op.toml`](operator.md), the recommended way to describe your operator). A name
from the config file's `[operators.NAME]` also works.

**Workload** ([concepts](concepts.md#workload))

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--preset NAME` | `small-files` (default), `large-objects`, `range-reads`, `list-stat` |
| `-c, --concurrency N` | concurrent operations |
| `-d, --duration DURATION` | the measurement window (`30s`, `2m`) |
| `--objects N` | dataset objects to generate |
| `--object-size SIZE` | size of each generated object (`16MiB`) |
| `--rate OPS` | open-loop arrival rate (operations per second, 0.001 to 1 000 000); latency counts from the intended start |
| `--existing PREFIX` | profile the objects already under `PREFIX`; writes nothing (implies `--read-only`) |
| `--seed N` | seed of the workload's random choices |
| `--set PATH=VALUE` | change one value of the operator or the workload, repeatable (`--set layers.retry.max_times=5`, `--set read.gap=1MiB`, `--set layers.cache=off`; [paths](operator.md#--set)) |

**Safety**

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--dry-run` | print the plan (requests, bytes, objects written and deleted, ETA, budgets; a warning when it would spend one) and exit (`-o json`: `schemas/plan.json`) |
| `--read-only` | refuse every write and delete (exit 5) |
| `--max-requests N` | send at most this many HTTP requests to the target (calls, for `fs://` and `memory://`), retries and the dataset upload included; the next one is not sent (exit 4) |
| `--max-bytes SIZE` | transfer at most this many body bytes, up and down, e.g. `10GiB`; a request body that does not fit is not sent, a download is cut where it crosses the budget, and a dataset larger than the budget is refused before it is uploaded (exit 4) |
| `--max-duration DURATION` | stop after this much wall time, e.g. `5m` (exit 4) |

A budget that stops a run cuts what is in flight, aborts the multipart uploads it interrupted,
saves the partial run and cleans up. Budgets cover the whole command: every operator of the
run, and every phase but cleanup (see [concepts](concepts.md)). `[defaults.budgets]` in the
config file sets defaults. Ctrl-C, SIGTERM and SIGHUP stop a run the same way (exit 130).

```bash
oprobe run s3://bucket/oprobe
oprobe run op.toml --preset range-reads -c 16 -d 1m
oprobe run s3://a/x 'r2://b/x?account_id=ACCOUNT_ID' --set layers.concurrent_limit.http=32
oprobe run prod --existing data/2026/ --max-requests 50000
```

## `oprobe demo`

`oprobe run lab://demo`, with the same workload and safety flags as `run`. Every 40th request
of the lab is a straggler that waits 250 ms, and it throttles above 40 requests in flight. Its default
workload is small files (64 × 64 KiB) with 16 workers for 8 s; `oprobe prove last` then proves
the top finding's remedy in about a minute.

## `oprobe prove RUN [FINDING]`

A/B-test a change of a run's operator. The change is the remedy of `FINDING` (default: the top
finding), or `--with`. When the remedy has a size, short trials pick it first. Then the current
operator and the changed one run interleaved until a sequential test decides on the objective, or
the budget ends. Prints the proven layer diff (Rust and TOML) with its evidence; `-o json` prints
the prove result (`schemas/prove.json`). Exit 3 when the change is worse on the objective.

The proof is made of **trials**: short runs of the current operator (A) and the changed one (B),
plus the sizing trials. It starts by printing how many trials it may take and the ETA of the
whole proof; `--dry-run` prints the same estimate (and the plan of one trial) and sends nothing.

A verdict other than `inconclusive` needs at least **3 pairs** of trials (one A and one B). The
orders are balanced in blocks of two pairs, one `AB` and one `BA`, and which comes first in a
block is drawn from the run's seed (`notes` says so). When the
budget allows fewer, the verdict is `inconclusive` (exit 0) with a note. When no pair ran at all,
the text says `not measured` and prints no diff; `-o json` still prints a valid result
(`verdict: "inconclusive"`, `pairs_count: 0`, a note). When the changed operator's trials
throttle more than `--max-throttle` allows, and more than the current operator's by more than
that allowance (beyond chance), the verdict is `inconclusive` too, with a note: the service's
limit, not the change, set what was measured. Throttling the change did not cause passes: a
service that answers 503 whatever the operator does (`lab://noisy`) throttles both alike.

Sizing follows the same bound. A remedy for throttling (`throttling`, `rate_limit`) is sized
among the values whose trials stay within `--max-throttle`; any other remedy among the values
that add no more than `--max-throttle` to what the run already had. When no value qualifies,
the least throttled one is tested and a note says so ("no value met --max-throttle"); the rule
above still decides the verdict.

The same holds for failures, on either objective: a changed operator whose operations fail more
than the run allows (1 %), and more than the current operator's, is `inconclusive` with a note
(a timeout that fails the slow operations lowers the p99 and improves nothing). A pair in which
a trial has no objective to compare (no successful operation, or nothing measured) is not
judged: the proof stops there and a note says so.

When the proof stops early because more pairs would not help, a note names the smallest change
its planned pairs could have shown at the noise it measured. On `--objective p99`, when the
latencies around a trial's p99 differ by more than 2×, a note says `p99 sits on a cliff: lengthen
the trial`: pass a longer `--trial`, so that each trial has enough operations to place its p99.

`prove` refuses a run that cannot be judged on performance (its first finding is `invalid_run`:
it failed, or it is partial and too short); profile the operator again first.

The verdict is whether the objective's interval excludes no change. The interval is on the
paired log ratios of the objective (B over A, pair by pair):

- Its estimate is the mean of the `AB` pairs' mean and the `BA` pairs' mean, so an effect of the
  order itself (the second trial of a pair running better or worse) cancels.
- Its spread is no smaller than the noise floor: the spread a pair's ratio would have from the
  trial-to-trial spread of A and of B alone, each learned from that side's consecutive trials
  (until B has two trials, it is assumed as noisy as A: the A/A spread; a floor learned from a
  single A/A difference is doubled).
- It is sequential: `prove` looks after every pair from the third on, and the interval of each
  look is as wide as the plan of `--pairs` looks requires, so that the verdict is wrong about a
  change that is none in fewer than 5 % of proofs, whenever the proof stops. A plan of more
  pairs therefore needs clearer evidence at its early looks. `pairs_max_count` in the result is
  that plan.

Shares, such as throttled requests, are compared with Newcombe's interval; the secondary
metrics' intervals are plain 95 % intervals on each metric's own trial-to-trial spread, shown
and never decisive. After an early stop the estimate overstates the change on average (the
proof stopped because it was large); the interval's coverage holds.

The ETA printed first is learned from the run being proved: what it took around its warm-up and
window, how long its last operations kept retrying after the window, and a cool-down per
throttled trial. The first pair corrects it when it was off. Under `--max-duration` the line
says how many trials the budget is estimated to fit; the proof runs every trial that really
fits.

A trial that ends throttled (429/503) is followed by a cool-down before the next trial starts:
the longest `Retry-After` it saw, at least twice the trial warm-up (250 ms to 2 s), at most 5 s.
The cool-down counts in the budget, Ctrl-C interrupts it, and `notes` says how often it
happened.

`--max-duration` is the one wall-time budget of the whole proof: no trial starts that would not
end within it, and no cool-down is waited past it (a pair whose second trial no longer fits
after the first one's cool-down is left incomplete and out of the result). When a budget (`--max-duration`, `--max-requests`, `--max-bytes`) stops the prove
part-way, it still prints and saves the partial result (`budget_exceeded: true`, usually
`inconclusive`) and exits 4; its trials stay attached, so `oprobe show --rm PROVE` removes them.

`RUN` is a run id, an id prefix, `last`, `last~N` or a run's `.oprobe` file. A production trace
has no workload to replay: `prove` refuses it and prints the `oprobe run` command for the service
it recorded. `FINDING` is a finding code (`throttling`, `tail_stragglers`, …); a finding whose
remedy is not a layer (`key_limit`, `client_bound`, a bandwidth cap on reads) has nothing to prove,
and `prove` refuses it with where to look instead. A finding's `next` command names the objective
its remedy is proved on: `--objective p99` for `throttling` and `rate_limit` (a cap takes the
throttled operations' backoffs out of the tail; it cannot raise goodput while spare workers keep
the service at its limit). The objective's change prints with its 95 % interval
([glossary](concepts.md#glossary)).

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--with PATH=VALUE` | the change to prove instead of the finding's remedy, repeatable |
| `--objective goodput\|p99` | what the change is judged on: successful operations (or bytes) per second (default), or the worst per-operation p99 latency |
| `--max-throttle RATIO` | share of throttled requests a change may cause, e.g. `0.1%` or `0.001` |
| `--trial DURATION` | measurement window of one trial (default `2s`, at most the run's own window) |
| `--pairs N` | A/B pairs at most, 3 to 12 (default 6); a value outside that range is a usage error (exit 2) |
| `--max-duration DURATION` | wall-time budget of the whole proof, e.g. `5m` |
| `--save FILE\|OPERATOR` | when the verdict is `improved`, write the proven change to an `op.toml` file or to `[operators.OPERATOR]` in the config file. A new file gets the operator with its `${ENV}` references and without secret values; the run's own `op.toml` (or another of the same service) is patched in place; the config file's path saves to the run's `[operators.NAME]`. Any other existing file is refused before a trial runs. The proof is saved first: a save that fails is a note |
| `--dry-run` | print the number of trials and the ETA of the whole proof, and exit (`-o json`: `schemas/prove-plan.json`) |
| `--read-only` | refuse every write and delete (exit 5) |
| `--max-requests N`, `--max-bytes SIZE` | send at most this many HTTP requests or body bytes, over every trial (exit 4) |

Every trial is saved as a run, a child of the prove, and hidden from `show --list`. A prove
stopped before its result is saved (Ctrl-C) deletes its trials.

```bash
oprobe prove last throttling
oprobe prove last throttling --save op.toml
oprobe prove last --with layers.tail_cut=on --objective p99
oprobe prove 20261122-0915 small_ranges --max-duration 10m
```

## `oprobe show [RUN|FILE]…`

Print a profile: a stored run, or a file (`.oprobe` from `run` or from
[`oprobe-trace`](embedding.md), or a report `.json`). Without an argument, the last run.
Pass two or more runs or files to compare them side by side on goodput, bandwidth, latency,
retries, throttling and stage split (`-o json`: the `run` document, `schemas/run.json`, `--detail` adds the per-API
comparison table). `-o json` for one run prints the shown run (`schemas/show.json`: the report of `schemas/report.json`, where it is stored, and the `by` and `range` sections when asked for); `--list -o json` the run list
(`schemas/run-list.json`; `-n` limits the runs and the proves alike), and `--rm -o json` the deleted ids (`schemas/removed.json`). A prove id, unambiguous prove prefix, `last-prove`, or `.prove.json` file (`show --list`
lists them) prints that prove's stored result as `prove` printed it (`schemas/prove.json`), also
after its run was removed.

A trace from `oprobe-trace` is recognised by its content, whatever its name. Its report has
`run.source = "trace"` and shows `production trace` where a run shows its workload. Its
operations are the application's OpenDAL calls (keys hashed), and the findings a trace supports
are derived: errors, throttling, hung requests, stragglers, cold connections, small ranges, slow
multipart and repeated reads (not bandwidth cap or client bound). `prove` refuses a trace
(exit 2): it needs a run oprobe drove.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--list` | list the stored runs (prove trials hidden) and the proves; a long change is cut in the list (`show PROVE` prints it whole) |
| `--all` | with `--list`: include the prove trials |
| `--rm RUN…` | delete stored runs (a run named twice is deleted once) |
| `--detail` | every section of the profile: the timeline (one row per interval of 1 s, or 10 s after ten minutes; long runs merge rows), the spread of the requests over keys, sizes, prefixes and remotes, the operator and the five slowest operations |
| `--by stage\|api\|conn` | group the requests by stage, storage API or connection |
| `--since DURATION` | only the time range from this far into the window: its goodput, latency quantiles, failures, requests, retries and throttling, where the time went, the verbs, the requests by API and the slowest operations, recomputed from the trace rows (`-o json`: the `range` object). With `--by`, only the range's requests are grouped. In an open-loop run (`--rate`), the arrivals due in the range that never started are counted (`missed_arrivals_count`) and count in its percentiles, each at the least it waited, as in the whole run: the percentiles are then "at least" values, printed with `≥` (`latency_at_least`) |
| `--until DURATION` | only the time range up to this far into the window (default: its end) |

An operation counts in the range it started in, a request in the range it was sent in. When the
run kept only a share of its rows, the range says so: its counts are estimates and its quantiles
weighted by the operations each row stands for.

```bash
oprobe show --list
oprobe show last --since 3s --until 8s
oprobe show last --by stage
oprobe show prod.oprobe --detail
oprobe show --rm last~3 last~4
```

## `oprobe lab [SCENARIO]`

Serve a local S3-compatible lab with faults until Ctrl-C and print its endpoint (`-o json`:
`schemas/lab.json`). Point any S3 client at it, or use `lab://SCENARIO` as an operator to start one
inside a run.

Scenarios (the same six as the app's): `demo`, `throttle`, `stragglers`, `bandwidth`, `flaky`,
`ratelimit`. Without one, the lab has no faults.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--bind ADDR` | the address to listen on (default `127.0.0.1:9000`) |
| `--allow-remote` | allow binding to a non-loopback address (`0.0.0.0`, LAN IP); refused without this flag because the lab accepts static lab credentials without authentication |
| `--max-store-size SIZE` | (hidden from `--help`) cap total in-memory object bytes stored by the lab (default `8GiB`; returns `507 InsufficientStorage` above it) |

## Run references

`last` (the newest run), `last~N` (N runs before it), a full id (`20261122-091512-ab12`) or an
unambiguous id prefix. `show` also takes a path to a file.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | ok |
| 1 | runtime failure (auth, network, storage, internal) |
| 2 | usage or configuration error |
| 3 | `prove`: the change is worse on the objective |
| 4 | a budget stopped the command |
| 5 | a safety rail refused the command |
| 130 | interrupted (Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, SIGHUP) |

Errors carry a stable code (`-o json`: `{"type":"error","error":{"code":…}}`, schema
`schemas/error.json`); [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#error-codes) lists them.

## Environment

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OPROBE_OUTPUT` | default `-o` |
| `OPROBE_CONFIG` | the config file |
| `OPROBE_DATA_DIR` | where runs are stored (default `<data dir>/oprobe/`) |
| `NO_COLOR` | no colors |
| `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY` | the egress proxy, unless `http.proxy` is set |


<!-- source: docs/reading-the-profile.md -->

# Reading the profile

A profile comes in three shapes:

| | Command | For |
|---|---|---|
| The brief | `oprobe run …` (default output) | the answer: the verdict, at most three findings, the next command |
| The profile | `oprobe show [RUN\|FILE] [--detail] [--by stage\|api\|conn]` | the terminal, logs, issues |
| JSON | `-o json` on any command | scripts and agents ([`schemas/report.json`](../schemas/report.json)) |

The app's Profile view shows the same sections with charts ([app](app.md)).

## The brief

```text
[Attention] 2.4% of HeadObject, 2.4% of PutObject and 2.6% of GetObject requests wait far longer for
  the server's first byte than their peers (stragglers).
  lab://demo · small-files · 8.0 s · run 20261123-135409-4b57
  ▲ 1 tail_stragglers (high confidence) — 2.4% of HeadObject, 2.4% of PutObject and 2.6% of
      GetObject requests wait far longer for the server's first byte than their peers (stragglers).
      33 HeadObject stragglers wait ~260ms for the first byte against ~9.48ms for a typical
      HeadObject; 100 PutObject stragglers wait ~260ms for the first byte against ~9.55ms for a
      typical PutObject; 214 GetObject stragglers wait ~260ms for the first byte against ~9.54ms for
      a typical GetObject; operation p50 9.65ms · p99 261ms
      remedy: layers.tail_cut + layers.retry.min_delay — re-issue requests far slower than their
        peers, after a short retry backoff (TailCutLayer + RetryLayer::with_min_delay)
      next: oprobe prove 20261123-135409-4b57 tail_stragglers
  1733.6 ops/s · 97.6 MiB/s · p50 9.65ms · p99 261ms · errors 0.00%
  full profile: oprobe show 20261123-135409-4b57 --detail · terms: https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/blob/v9.3.3/docs/concepts.md#glossary
```

(`oprobe demo`; your numbers differ from run to run.)

- **The badge** is the verdict level: **OK**, **Review** (worth a look: informational
  findings, a partial run), **Attention** (warning findings), **Critical** (critical findings).
  JSON carries the same levels as `ok`, `review`, `attention`, `critical`.
- **The headline** says what bounds the operator on this workload: throttling, the server's
  latency, the network (connect, upload, download), queueing in the client, or the client itself.
- **Findings**: at most three, most severe first. Each has its code, the evidence in one line,
  its confidence, and the remedy as an `op.toml` path, with no number: only `prove` sizes a
  change.
- **Key numbers**: goodput (successful operations per second), throughput, latency percentiles.
- **Next**: the command that proves the top remedy.

## The profile

`oprobe show` prints these sections (`--detail` adds every column, the per-second timeline,
the configuration and the five slowest operations):

| Section | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| header | run id, operator, workload, window, concurrency, start time |
| verdict | the badge and where the time went, in one sentence |
| key numbers | goodput and throughput, latency p50/p99/p99.9/max, failed operations, throttled responses, and one **resilience** line: retries, time spent waiting between attempts, 429/503, the 5xx/4xx/network split and the top failure classes (the app's Retries section) |
| findings | every finding: code, cause, evidence, confidence, remedy |
| where the time goes | each operation's wall time split into stages (below) |
| operations | per workload verb: count, ops/s, p50, p99, max, requests per operation, errors (`--detail`: MiB/s, retries, throttled share) |
| backend requests | per storage API (`GetObject`, `PutObject`, …): count, share on warm connections, TTFB and total p50/p99, bytes down/up, status codes (`--detail`: every stage's p50/p99); and, for a run that wrote, a **writes** line: the multipart part size OpenDAL used (and the requested `write.chunk` and the service's part-size limits when it was clamped) and the parts uploaded with their mean size — the knobs `prove` sizes for `slow_multipart` |
| connections | HTTP version, TLS, the connections dialed during the warm-up and in the window, reuse, peak in-flight requests, dial time per phase (proxy CONNECT included), and a **tcp** line from the kernel: the minimum rtt (the network's own round trip) and the smoothed rtt p50/p99 (which on a fast network includes the server's delay and delayed acknowledgements), connections that retransmitted, the share of sending time limited by the peer's receive window or the local send buffer, the delivery rate. High rtt or retransmits point at the network; a clean network with a high TTFB points at the server. `--detail` adds the TLS handshakes (resumed share, HelloRetryRequests) and the cold start (dials and first operations before the warm-up absorbed them) |
| bytes | logical vs backend bytes, read amplification, over-read, requests per operation, cache hits, and the bytes on the wire (from the kernel's per-connection counters, when they were read) |
| slowest operations | the five worst operations request by request (waterfalls), with what each request recorded beyond its stages (below) and, with `--detail`, their async call stacks |
| self | the profiler's own health: scheduling lag, CPU, whether the client was saturated |
| cleanup | test data removed (verified), or what is left |

`--detail` also adds, per interval of the timeline, retries, new connections and the client's
CPU (percent of one core), and the first read and re-reads of a key to SPREAD (object sizes as
ranges; a column no row has, such as a hot key's errors, is left out). The timeline ends with
the measured window: what draining operations did after it counts in its last interval.

`--by stage` sums the requests' time per stage, `--by api` per storage API, `--by conn` per
connection (cold and warm, per remote address). A request belongs to the stage it spent most of
its time in, and the stages have one name everywhere (the groups of `--by stage`, the tail
split, the waterfalls, the report's fields): `queue`, `connect`, `send`, `ttfb`, `body`,
`stall`. Up to 9.2 `--by stage` and the waterfalls called the `body` stage `transfer`. `--by stage` also gives each stage's p50/p99
per API and, when the requests recorded them, the request signals below.

### Request signals

Besides its stage timings a request row can carry what the response and the connection said.
The waterfalls of the slowest operations (terminal and app) list them per request, and
`show --by stage` summarises them per API:

| Signal | What it says |
|---|---|
| error code, Retry-After | the provider's own error (`SlowDown`, `ServerBusy`) and how long it asked to wait |
| tail-cut, body incomplete | a request cancelled early by `TailCutLayer` hedging, or a response body dropped before EOF |
| h2 streams | HTTP/2 streams active on the connection during the request |
| upload acked, send buffered | when the kernel saw the last request byte acknowledged, and when the body reached the send buffer: the end of the upload |
| cache, edge, age | CDN cache status (`hit`, `miss`), edge PoP and object age |
| region, class, sse | the bucket's region (`x-amz-bucket-region`), storage class and server-side encryption |
| rtt, min rtt, retransmits, Server-Timing | the connection's round trip, minimum RTT and retransmitted segments, plus the server's own timing header |

The compact profile shows the error code, Retry-After, tail-cut/incomplete body status and cache
status; `--detail` shows every signal.

`--since 3s --until 8s` shows one time range of the window (a burst, the seconds a rate limit
bit): its numbers, where the time went, the verbs, the requests by API and its slowest
operations, recomputed from the trace rows. When the rows were sampled it says so, and each row
counts for the operations it stands for. In the app, drag across the timeline or the heatmap.

### Where the time goes

Each operation's wall time is split exactly; an instant counts once even when requests overlap:

| Stage | Time when … | If it dominates |
|---|---|---|
| queue | requests wait for a connection or an in-flight permit | a concurrency limit or a small pool; see `cold_connections` and `throttling` |
| connect | DNS, TCP, proxy and TLS of a new connection | connections are not reused, or the proxy or TLS is slow (`http.keep_alive`, `http.version`) |
| send | the request body goes out | upload bandwidth; `write.chunk`, `write.concurrent`. Uploads that share one saturated uplink are a `bandwidth_cap` (`layers.throttle.bandwidth`), not hung requests |
| TTFB | waiting for the first byte (the server's work plus one round trip) | the store or the distance to it; stragglers show as a long tail (`layers.tail_cut`). A TTFB that grows with the requests in flight, in a run that varied them at least twofold, is the service's queue: `throttling` without a 429/503 (below) |
| body | the response body arrives | download bandwidth per stream × streams; `read.chunk`, `read.concurrent`. Downloads that share one capped link are a `bandwidth_cap`, not hung requests; a body that stalls (far slower than the other bodies) is a hung request |
| stall | the body waits for your code to read it (client time: its own segment in a waterfall, never part of body) | the consumer, not storage |
| retry | the retry layer sleeps before the next attempt | throttling or errors; see the findings (`errors` on retried 5xx or lost connections: `layers.retry.min_delay`) |
| client | everything else: OpenDAL, signing, checksums | CPU (`client_bound`), tiny objects |

### How it is measured

- **Requests** are observed inside OpenDAL's own HTTP client (reqwest with rustls, exactly as
  OpenDAL builds it): a timed resolver, a connector layer that times each dial, the TLS
  ClientHello timestamp (which splits TCP from TLS), the response's connection identity (cold or
  warm), and the body timed as it arrives and as your code consumes it. Waiting inside reqwest's
  pool for an idle connection is part of TTFB. Kernel TCP statistics (RTT, retransmits) are read
  at the end of a request on Linux and macOS.
- **Operations** are the workload's logical calls (`read`, `write`, `stat`, `list`, a parquet
  scan); every request is attributed to the operation that caused it, including requests in
  OpenDAL's background tasks.
- **Open loop** (`--rate`): latency counts from the intended start, and arrivals that never
  started count in every percentile as censored values, so a slow server cannot hide behind fewer
  requests. A censored value is a lower bound (the arrival had waited that long when the window
  ended; nothing says how much longer it would have taken), so those percentiles are "at least"
  values. When more than 1 % of the scheduled arrivals never completed, the p99 has no upper
  bound at all (its rank falls among the censored arrivals): the open loop **stalled**. No limit
  is needed to judge that. The headline leads with it ("1808 of 3000 scheduled arrivals never
  completed (60.3%): the p99 is at least 1.80s and has no upper bound"), the profile's `checks`
  line and `verdict.sla.breaches` carry the same sentence, and the verdict is Critical. The
  bound is the run's own p99. The finding beside it says who fell behind: the service, when it
  queues (`throttling`), or the client (`client_bound`).
- **A service that queues** (`throttling` with no 429/503) is read from timing alone, so it is
  held to more than a rejection is. The time to first byte is fitted against the requests in
  flight with one service time per storage API (a HEAD is quicker than a ranged GET at any
  load); the run must have varied its requests in flight at least twofold; the wait the model
  puts at the busiest level must be more than twice the client's own scheduling lag (`self`),
  which also grows with the requests in flight; and a run whose client was saturated has no
  such finding. Its remedy is advice: a cap on the requests in flight
  (`layers.concurrent_limit.http`) moves the wait from the service's queue to the client's. It
  shortens no operation and adds no throughput, so there is nothing for `prove` to measure, and
  `prove` refuses it. A run at a steady load shows no queue: its headline says the load was
  not varied. Vary it with `--set shape=ramp:FROM..TO/D` (arrivals per second, over `D`).
- **An open loop that fell behind** with CPU to spare kept every worker busy, so a steady one
  shows a single level of requests in flight: nothing in it tells a service at its capacity
  from too few workers, and `client_bound` says exactly that ("this run cannot tell") instead
  of advising more workers. A run that varied its load can tell: when the time to first byte
  grew with the requests in flight, the service queues (`throttling`, as above, and no
  `client_bound`); when it stayed put from half the requests in flight to all of them, the
  service had room and the workers are the bound (`client_bound`: raise `-c`).
- **Percentiles** are exact when every operation was kept, otherwise from histograms with three
  significant digits. Counts always agree with the totals. The report keeps the run's whole
  latency distribution (`latency_histogram`, 20 bins per decade), and the latency distribution
  (in the app a tail plot: the share of operations slower than each latency, on log axes) is
  drawn from it whenever the trace rows are sampled.
- **The timeline** has one row per interval (1 s for the first ten minutes, then 10 s).
  Operations, goodput (`goodput_ops_per_s`: successes only; `ops_per_s` counts every attempt)
  and the latency quantiles belong to the interval an operation *started* in; requests
  (`requests_count`, retries included), throttled responses (`throttled_count`), retries and
  failures (`errors_count`) to the interval they *happened* in, so a 503 at +7 s is drawn at
  +7 s. `ops_count` says how many operations stand behind an interval's quantiles: a p99 needs
  about 1 000. Each interval also carries the same counters per verb (`verbs`).
- **The profiler's cost** is measured: `cargo bench -p oprobe-trace --bench overhead` compares
  the same operations with and without the layer (budget 2 µs per operation), and the profile's
  `self` section reports scheduling lag and CPU during the run. A run where the client was
  saturated says so, and its verdict is `client_bound` rather than a server limit.

## JSON

`-o json` prints one document on stdout. `run` and `show` print the report
(`"schema": "oprobe.report/7"`), `prove` the prove result (`"schema": "oprobe.prove/9"`),
