`show --list` the run list. Numeric fields carry their unit in the name (`_ms`, `_bytes`,
`_ratio`, `_count`), enums are `snake_case`, and fields are only ever added within 9.x. Errors are
`{"type":"error","error":{"code","message","hint","retryable","docs"}}`.

## Files

A stored run lives in `<data dir>/oprobe/runs/` as one `.oprobe` file (format `oprobe.run/7`: a
zstd stream of the header with the operator spec and workload, columnar segments of operation and
request rows, the per-second timeline, and the report). `oprobe-trace` writes `oprobe.trace/9`
files (one JSON document: the aggregates, service posture and sampled rows). `oprobe show FILE`
and the app open both, as well as standalone `.prove.json` (`oprobe.prove/9`) files.

A run file keeps every row up to `max_requests` rows (`[defaults]`, 1 000 000). Past that the
rows are thinned, each kept row carrying the operations it stands for; failed and throttled
operations are kept in full for twice as long, then thinned the same way. However long the run
and whatever it met, the file stays within what `show` and the app read (4 GiB of rows): a run
that reaches that keeps its aggregates exact and stops keeping rows.


<!-- source: docs/embedding.md -->

# Profiling production: `oprobe-trace`

`oprobe-trace` is oprobe's instrumentation as one
OpenDAL layer. Add it to the operator your service already uses, and every backend request is
timed by stage and aggregated in bounded memory. Save a `.oprobe` file and open it with
`oprobe show FILE` or in the app, like any run.

It is the only crate oprobe publishes, and it has a semver promise.

**Requirements.** OpenDAL 0.59 (`opendal` or `opendal-core`; another minor shows up as trait
errors about `Layer` or `Servicer`), the Tokio runtime, Rust 1.91 or later (OpenDAL 0.59's own
minimum; the oprobe workbench itself needs 1.97), and, for the `otel` feature, `opentelemetry`
0.32 (the version OpenDAL's `opendal-layer-otelmetrics` uses, so both layers share one global
meter).

## Three lines

```toml
[dependencies]
oprobe-trace = { git = "https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe", tag = "v9.3.3" }
```

`oprobe-trace` is not on crates.io yet: the git dependency above is the one that resolves today
(pin the tag of the release you read this from). Once a release publishes it, the same version
is `oprobe-trace = "9"`.

```rust
let (layer, handle) = oprobe_trace::layer(oprobe_trace::Config::default());
let op = Operator::new(builder)?.layer(layer);
handle.save("prod.oprobe")?;          // then: oprobe show prod.oprobe
```

Apply it first, before your other layers (`ConcurrentLimitLayer`, `TailCutLayer`, `RetryLayer`): it
installs the instrumented `HttpTransport` on `OperationContext`, and the layers above it then wrap
it, so HTTP concurrency caps stay in force and every retry is recorded as its own request. The
order matters, and so does a client of your own: see [Where the layer goes](#where-the-layer-goes).
Give OpenDAL's retry layer the handle's notifier, so retries land in the profile's Retries section
(count, backoff, throttling) and the attempts of one call count as one operation:

```rust
let (trace, handle) = oprobe_trace::layer(oprobe_trace::Config::default());
let op = Operator::new(builder)?
    .layer(trace)
    .layer(RetryLayer::new().with_notify(handle.retry_notify()));
```

Without the notifier every attempt is an operation of its own, and retries are not counted.
When you use a local cache layer (`FoyerLayer`, `MokaLayer`), wrap it with `handle.cache_layer()`
so cache hits, hit bytes and lookup latency are recorded in `snapshot.cache` and `snapshot.bytes`:

```rust
let op = op.layer(foyer_layer).layer(handle.cache_layer());
```

## Where the layer goes

DNS, TCP, TLS and connection statistics can only be measured from inside the HTTP client. So by
default the layer brings its own client (built like OpenDAL's default one) and **replaces the
HTTP transport installed on the operator**. OpenDAL composes transports in the order of the
`.layer(...)` calls: each layer receives the transport the layers before it left, and wraps or
replaces it. Two things follow:

- **Layers that wrap the transport go after the trace layer.**
  `ConcurrentLimitLayer::with_http_concurrent_limit` added *after* the trace layer wraps the
  instrumented client and limits it. Added *before*, it wraps a transport the trace layer then
  replaces, and silently stops limiting. Add `handle.queue_layer()` last, and the time requests
  wait for the limiter is their `queue` stage:

  ```rust
  let op = Operator::new(builder)?
      .layer(trace)                                                   // first
      .layer(ConcurrentLimitLayer::new(64).with_http_concurrent_limit(16))
      .layer(RetryLayer::new().with_notify(handle.retry_notify()))
      .layer(handle.queue_layer());                                   // last
  ```

- **A client of your own is not used.** A transport you installed with
  `Operator::with_context(OperationContext::new().with_http_transport(..))`, or the process
  default of `HttpTransporter::install_default`, is replaced too, with its proxy, TLS roots,
  timeouts and pool settings. Either say the same on `Config` (`proxy`, `extra_ca_pem`,
  `http_version`, `keep_alive`, `max_inflight`; see [Configuration](#configuration)), or keep your
  client:

```rust
let cfg = oprobe_trace::Config::default().keep_http_transport(true);
let (trace, handle) = oprobe_trace::layer(cfg);
let op = Operator::new(builder)?
    .with_context(OperationContext::new().with_http_transport(my_client))
    .layer(ConcurrentLimitLayer::new(64).with_http_concurrent_limit(16)) // before or after: both work
    .layer(trace);
```

With **`keep_http_transport(true)`** the layer wraps the installed transport instead of replacing
it: your client, and every limiter beneath the trace layer, carries the requests unchanged,
wherever the layer sits. The layer then sees each request from outside:

| | the instrumented client (default) | `keep_http_transport(true)` |
|---|---|---|
| queue, time to first byte, body, consumer stall | yes | yes |
| status, bytes, request IDs, provider error codes, retries, operations | yes | yes |
| DNS, TCP, proxy and TLS time, upload send time | yes | no: part of the time to first byte |
| connections: reuse, dials, TLS details, kernel TCP statistics | yes | no |
| your proxy, TLS roots, timeouts, pool | no: set them on `Config` | yes |

`format!("{trace:?}")` says which one a layer does (`http_transport: "replaced by the
instrumented client"` or `"the installed transport, observed"`).

What was not observed is not reported as a number. With `keep_http_transport(true)`:
- `Snapshot::connections` counts the requests by protocol, and nothing else:
  `connections.observed()` is false, and `dialed`, `reused_requests` and `reuse_pct` say nothing
  (until 9.2 every answered request counted as reused: "100 %"). `oprobe show FILE` prints
  `dials not observed · reuse not observed`.
- The file's `service` says `"http_transport": "installed"` and leaves out `http_version` and
  `keep_alive`, which describe the instrumented client (the client is yours).
- A request row has `conn_id` 0, and its time to first byte includes connecting and sending the
  body: a slow upload shows as a long `ttfb`, not as a slow server.

## What you get

Every OpenDAL call is one **operation**, linked to the backend requests it issued, as in a run
oprobe drives: `stat`, `read.full` / `read.range` (one `open` until its stream ends, or one ranged
read), `write` / `write.multipart` (the writer's life), `list`, `delete` (a batch), `copy`,
`rename`, `create_dir`. So a trace has verbs, operation latency and where its time went (queue,
backend, retry, client), the slowest operations with their requests, hot keys and prefixes, size
buckets, cold and warm reads, and over-read. A call your code drops (a timeout, a cancelled
future) is recorded as `cancelled`. Keys are recorded hashed: see [The file](#the-file).

- **`handle.snapshot()`**: a `Snapshot` with the aggregates so far: per storage API and stage
  (queue, connect, send, TTFB, body, stall; count, mean, p50/p90/p99/p99.9/max), per verb,
  connection reuse and dial times, retries and status codes, bytes, a timeline. Aggregates are
  exact.
- **`handle.save(path)`**: a `.oprobe` profile: the snapshot plus a sample of whole operations
  with their requests (failed, throttled and slowest ones are always kept, within
  `Config::max_rows`). The rows saved are moved out of memory, so periodic saves hold the
  operations of each period; the aggregates are cumulative. `snapshot.save(path)` writes the
  aggregates alone.
- **`handle.save_and_reset(path)`**: the same, then a fresh window: the aggregates start again
  from zero (atomically with the snapshot), so hourly files are hourly profiles.
- **`Exporter`**: called for every request as it completes, on the request path (keep it cheap).

```rust
struct Slow;
impl oprobe_trace::Exporter for Slow {
    fn on_request(&self, r: &oprobe_trace::RequestRecord) {
        if r.timing.ttfb_us > 500_000 {
            eprintln!("slow {} {} ttfb {} ms", r.method, r.api.label(), r.timing.ttfb_us / 1000);
        }
    }
}
let cfg = oprobe_trace::Config::default().exporter(std::sync::Arc::new(Slow));
```

- **OpenTelemetry** (feature `otel`, `opentelemetry` 0.32): `oprobe_trace::otel::config(&meter)`
  records two histograms, in seconds:
  - `http.client.request.duration`, the standard metric of the HTTP semantic conventions:
    **exactly once per HTTP request**, with standard attributes only (`http.request.method`,
    `server.address`, `server.port`, and `http.response.status_code`,
    `network.protocol.version`, `error.type` when they apply). Its count is the number of
    requests, as any HTTP dashboard assumes.
  - `oprobe.http.client.request.stage.duration`: where each request's time went, once per stage
    that took time. `oprobe.stage` is `queue`, `connect`, `send`, `ttfb`, `body` or `stall`
    (they add up to the request's duration); it also carries `oprobe.api`,
    `http.request.method`, `http.response.status_code` and OpenDAL's own metric labels
    (`scheme`, `namespace`, `root`, `operation`), so its series join
    `opendal-layer-otelmetrics`'. `scheme`, `namespace` and `root` are those of the operator
    that issued the request: a layer cloned onto several operators labels each one's requests
    with its own (until 9.2, with the first operator's). Your own `Exporter` reads the same
    from `RequestRecord::service`.

  Backend calls of `memory` and `fs` are not HTTP requests and are in neither. Operation
  durations and cache metrics are not repeated: use OpenDAL's own metrics layers for them.
  (Until 9.1 the stages were recorded into `http.client.request.duration` itself, under
  `oprobe.stage`, so every request counted up to seven times; query the new histogram for them.)

## Configuration

`Config` is a builder; every setting has the default OpenDAL's own client has:

| Method | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `max_rows(n)` | 10 000 | request rows kept in memory (aggregates are exact regardless; 0 keeps aggregates only) |
| `http_version(v)` | `HttpVersion::Auto` | `Auto` (HTTP/1.1, as OpenDAL), `H1` or `H2` |
| `keep_alive(on)` | true | reuse connections |
| `max_inflight(n)` | unlimited | cap concurrent HTTP requests; waiting shows as `queue` |
| `extra_ca_pem(pem)` | none | trust an extra PEM bundle besides the system and WebPKI roots |
| `insecure_skip_verify(on)` | false | skip certificate verification (development only) |
| `proxy(Some(url) \| None)` | the environment | an explicit `http://` proxy, or none |
| `https(on)` | true | selects `HTTPS_PROXY` over `HTTP_PROXY` |
| `tcp_info(on)` | true | read kernel TCP statistics at the end of each request (Linux, macOS) |
| `keep_http_transport(on)` | false | wrap the operator's own HTTP transport instead of replacing it ([Where the layer goes](#where-the-layer-goes)); the client settings above then do not apply, `max_inflight` does |
| `exporter(e)` | none | your `Exporter` |

`handle.transport_error()` says why HTTP requests are not instrumented, if the transport could not
be built (an invalid proxy URL, a CA bundle that does not parse). The operator keeps working; only
in-process services (`memory`, `fs`) are observed then.

## How it works

For HTTP services the layer replaces the operator's `HttpTransport` with OpenDAL's own reqwest client
(rustls with aws-lc-rs, the same pool defaults: no connect timeout, unlimited idle connections per
host, 90 s idle timeout), observed through reqwest's public extension points: a timed DNS resolver,
a connector layer that times each dial, a TLS session store that timestamps the ClientHello, and a
body wrapper that times the transfer and your code's consumption. Nothing is decrypted or
proxied. For `memory` and `fs` it records one request per backend call.

A connection's dial belongs to the request that started it: that request is the connection's
cold one, whichever request is answered first on a shared HTTP/2 connection; a request that
waited for another's dial shows the wait as queue time (`detail.dial_wait_us`). A dial whose
request went elsewhere is a connection nobody waited for: counted, charged to no request.
Kernel TCP statistics are read at the end of each request, and the connection's retransmits
since the previous reading are charged to the requests in flight on it, so
`detail.retrans_count` adds up to the connection's count and no retransmit is charged twice:
- to the requests that are **sending a body**, when there are any (what a client retransmits
  is what it sends): an upload is charged its own retransmits, not the small GET that ends
  beside it on a shared HTTP/2 connection;
- else evenly to all of them (on HTTP/1.1 that is the one request).

A request counts as sending from the moment the transport can tell which connection carries
its body: with one upload in flight, the only connection alive, or, once the body is handed
to the kernel, the only one with unsent bytes in its send queue. With several uploads in
flight it cannot, and an upload joins at its response headers; a request that ends on the
same HTTP/2 connection before that is charged the upload's retransmits so far. An upload that
fails or is cancelled before any response carries the retransmits of its connection when that
connection was known.

The socket of a new connection is looked up on the runtime's blocking pool (one scan of the
descriptor table answers every connection dialed meanwhile), never on a worker thread, and no
request waits for it: a request reads the answer when its response headers arrive and again
when it ends. A request that ends before the lookup answered (the first request of a
connection, when the blocking pool is busy) has no kernel statistics; what its connection sent
and retransmitted counts with the connection's next request. Connection ids (`conn_id`) number
the client's connections in the order they were dialed, from 1.

A response OpenDAL cannot use (a `Content-Encoding` or `Content-Length` that does not parse)
fails the operation and is recorded as a failed request, not to be retried.

Above the transport, the layer wraps the service: each call runs in an operation scope that the
transport (and OpenDAL's background tasks, through a scope-propagating executor) reports its
requests to. The memory stays bounded however long the process lives: rows are sampled within
`Config::max_rows`, and past about 2 000 intervals the oldest timeline intervals are merged in
pairs (a month-long trace keeps under 2 000 intervals, the recent ones at full resolution).

`oprobe show FILE` marks the report `run.source = "trace"` and shows `production trace` instead
of a workload. Its findings are `errors`, `throttling` (and `rate_limit`, `key_limit`),
`hung_requests`, `tail_stragglers`, `cold_connections`, and, from the operations,
`small_ranges`, `slow_multipart` (when the operations issued their requests one after another)
and `repeated_reads`. The ones that need a load oprobe varied or its own client are not:
`bandwidth_cap` and `client_bound`. A trace has no workload to replay, so `oprobe prove` refuses
it. Reproduce the traffic with `oprobe run OPERATOR` and prove that run.

## Overhead

```bash
cargo bench -p oprobe-trace --bench overhead              # ~10 s
cargo bench -p oprobe-trace --bench overhead -- --quick   # ~1 s, runs in CI
```

The bench runs the same operations on a plain operator and on a traced one, interleaved, and
reports the median difference per operation: on `memory://`, and over HTTP against a local server
(OpenDAL's `http` service: OpenDAL's own reqwest client against the layer's instrumented one).
The budget is **2 µs per operation** for the layer's bookkeeping, measured on `memory://`; the
bench fails above it. On a 4-core Linux VM (busy with other builds):

```text
oprobe-trace overhead on memory:// (31 rounds × 50000 ops)
  plain OpenDAL         1.032 µs/op
  with oprobe-trace     2.363 µs/op
  overhead              1.322 µs/op  (p10 1.119, p90 1.547; budget 2 µs)
oprobe-trace overhead over HTTP on loopback (31 rounds × 4000 ops)
  plain OpenDAL        19.874 µs/op
  with oprobe-trace    25.222 µs/op
  overhead              5.167 µs/op  (p10 0.979, p90 8.327)
```

`memory://` is the worst case: its backend call costs well under a microsecond, so the difference
is all bookkeeping (an operation and its request). Over HTTP the transport's hooks add a few
microseconds to a request; against object storage, where a request takes milliseconds, the layer
is lost in the noise.

## Stability

Within 9.x the API documented on docs.rs is stable: changes are additive. A trace file is read
by the oprobe of the version that wrote it; reading the files of another version is not
promised. Public structs and enums are `#[non_exhaustive]`,
so read fields freely but build `Config` with its methods. The `__internal` feature exists for the
oprobe binary and has no semver promise; do not enable it.

## The file

`oprobe.trace/9` is one JSON document, readable without oprobe:

```text
{ "format": "oprobe.trace/9", "oprobe_trace_version": "9.3.2", "created_at": "…",
  "service": { "scheme": "s3", "name": "my-bucket", "root": "/data/", "http_version": "auto", "keep_alive": true },
  "snapshot": { … }, "rows": { "ops": [ … ], "reqs": [ … ], "info": { … }, "sampling": { … } } }
```

`service` is the OpenDAL service the layer was applied to: its scheme, name (the bucket or
container), root and client posture (`http_version`, `keep_alive`, `max_inflight_count`), with no
credentials or options. A bare `snapshot.save` has neither `service` nor `rows`.
`rows.ops` are the operations (each carrying its exact sampling `weight` when thinned); each
request row names its operation (`op_id`), its strongly typed storage `api`, the length of the
byte range it asked for (`detail.range_bytes`) and, when it failed, its class
(`storage.condition_not_match`, `storage.already_exists`, `storage.conflict`,
`storage.range_not_satisfied`, `storage.throttled`, …) and whether the failure is temporary
(`detail.temporary`).

**Keys are hashed.** An operation's `key` is its first path segment (at most 32 bytes) and a
48-bit hash of the whole key: `logs/2026/11/a.parquet` is recorded as `logs/#3f2a…`. Prefixes and
hot keys still slice the traffic, and repeated reads are still told apart, but the file never
holds a key. Request IDs and remote addresses can be in it; credentials never are: an error
text loses the credentials of every URL in it (`user:password@`, the signature of a presigned
URL, an SAS `sig`, STS and access tokens) when it is recorded, before any exporter, snapshot or
file sees it, and the errors the instrumented client returns to your code quote URLs the same
way. Treat a profile like a log file before you paste it into an issue.


<!-- source: docs/app.md -->

# The app

`oprobe` with no command opens the app, built on [Native Shell (nsh)](https://github.com/longbridge/nsh):
a native window when there is a display, the same app in the terminal otherwise (also over SSH).

```bash
oprobe          # the app
```

| Where | Drawn with | Comes with |
|---|---|---|
| macOS 14+ | AppKit, Core Animation, CoreText | the `.pkg`, the `.dmg` (`oprobe.app`), the macOS archives |
| Windows 10 1809+ | Win32, Direct2D, DirectWrite | the `.msi` (Start menu entry), the Windows archives |
| Linux (GTK 4.14+) | GTK 4, Pango | `oprobe-desktop-<ver>-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz`, or `cargo install` with `--features gui` ([install](install.md#from-source)) |
| any terminal | the nsh terminal backend | every build except the CLI-only archives |

Linux packages for servers (`.deb`, `.rpm`, the static musl archives) have the app in the
terminal and need no GTK. The CLI-only archives (`oprobe-cli-…`, `install.sh --cli`) have no app
at all.

The app has no logic of its own: it calls the same service layer as the CLI (`run`, `prove`,
`show`), so a run started in the app is a run in `oprobe show --list`, and the reverse.

## The window

The window works like other professional tools on your platform (design:
[app-native](design/app-native.md)):

- **Sidebar**:
  - Lists the runs, newest first, grouped under their operator. Each row shows the verdict, the
    run's short id, the preset, when it ran, and its goodput and p99.
  - Runs started from the app, the CLI or another window show up here.
  - A running job is the first row, with its progress.
  - Click a run to show it. With ⌘ (macOS) or Ctrl held, a click adds or removes a run; with
    Shift held, it extends the selection.
  - The runs are one list for the keyboard (one Tab stop) and for screen readers (a list of
    options, the selected ones said so): ↑ / ↓ move the selection, Shift+↑ / ↓ extend it,
    Home / End go to the ends, typing a run's short id, operator or preset finds it, Return
    opens it, and Delete (⌘⌫ on macOS) asks to delete the selection.
  - The selection looks like the platform's: filled with the accent on macOS (grey while the
    list or the window is not active), a subtle fill with an accent mark on Windows and Linux.
  - Two or more selected runs show **Compare**.
  - Secondary-click a run for its menu: Open, Compare With Selected, Prove…, Copy Run ID,
    Copy Command and Delete…. The row the menu acts on is outlined while it is open.
  - Drag the sidebar's edge to resize it. Its width, whether it shows, the page (Profile or
    Operator) and, on macOS and Windows, the window's size and position are restored at the
    next start.
  - On macOS it is drawn on the window's sidebar material, on Windows 11 on Mica; elsewhere it
    has its own colour.
- **Toolbar**: it sits in the title bar, at the platform's height. It holds the run's id and
  operator, the **Profile / Operator** switch, **New Run** (＋), and **Run Again** ▶, which
  becomes **Stop** ■ while a job runs. On Windows and Linux it also holds the main menu (⋯ or ☰),
  which opens under its button: New Run…, Open Run File…, Show/Hide Sidebar, Full Screen,
  Preferences (Settings on Windows), the documentation, About oprobe, and Quit (Exit on
  Windows).
- **Menus**: on macOS the menu bar holds oprobe, File, Edit, Run, View, Window and Help. Every
  item, the system's own (Undo, Quit, …) included, is in the app's language. On Windows and
  Linux the same menus' shortcuts work under the hidden title bar. Shortcuts that a text field
  also uses (Delete, ⌘⌫) are left to the field while you type, and the menus' actions wait while
  a dialog is open.
- **New Run** (mod+N) is a dialog: the operator (a URL, an `op.toml`, a configured name) with a
  **Choose** pop-up that lists the lab's scenarios, the operators of your config file
  (`[operators.NAME]`), the `op.toml` files you ran before and **Choose op.toml…**; the workload
  (a pop-up); the duration, concurrency and an optional read-only **Existing prefix**. The operator field has the focus when it opens,
  Return anywhere presses the default button and Escape cancels. A `lab://` run starts at once;
  a real target is **planned first**: **Review Plan** shows what the run will write, read and
  delete (and under which prefix), how long it takes and the budgets that stop it, and only then
  does the button become **Run**. Changing the form drops the plan.
- **Run Again** (mod+R) repeats the selected run as it ran: its operator, its whole workload
  (the open-loop rate, the dataset, the seed, the key popularity, …) and every operator value
  the run set on top of its operator (the `op.toml` file or the configured operator is read
  again; for a URL, what is not the default of the URL). A `lab://` run starts at once. A real
  target opens New Run on its plan: the fields show the run's operator, workload, duration,
  concurrency and existing prefix, and **Runs again as** shows the command of the run the form
  will start, as it stands now. Change the duration, the concurrency or the prefix and only
  that changes. Choose another workload and the operator's values stay (its endpoint, its
  layers: the run still goes where it went), while the rate, the dataset and the seed of the
  old workload go. Choose another operator and it is a new run, with nothing carried over.
  Secrets are never stored in a run: they come from the operator's file, the config file or
  the environment, as for any run.
- **Opening a file** (`.oprobe`, a trace, a report): a file is read as untrusted input. A run
  file may hold blocks of at most 256 MiB, decompress to at most 4 GiB and its rows may take
  at most 4 GiB of memory (about nine times the default cap of a million rows); a file beyond
  that, or one that claims more than it holds, is refused with an error, never opened halfway.
- **Settings** (mod+,): the language, where runs are stored and the config file. Each change
  applies at once. On macOS it is a window of its own; on Windows and Linux a preferences dialog
  with a close button; in a terminal a dialog.
- **About oprobe**: the version and links (the system's About panel on macOS).
- **Delete** asks first with the system's alert (Cancel is the default button). The runs go to
  oprobe's trash (`<data>/trash/`), not away: **Undo** in the notice bar brings them back. Once
  the notice goes, the folder goes on to the system's trash where there is one; oprobe's trash
  is emptied after a week. `oprobe show --rm` in the CLI still deletes for good.
- **Quitting** (⌘Q, Ctrl+Q, Exit, or the window's close button) while a run or a prove goes on
  asks first: **Stop and Quit** stops it, or Cancel keeps it running. The app then waits for
  the job to remove its test data, showing what it is doing and for how long, and quits by
  itself when that is done. It waits 60 s at most (an abort of a multipart upload may take
  30 s to give up on a service that does not answer, and the cleanup gets as long again).
  Past that it says which job was left and that objects under its `oprobe-run-…/` prefix may
  remain on the target (the next run against the same target removes them), and offers
  **Quit Anyway**; the same line goes to the log file. In a terminal, Ctrl+C waits the same
  way and prints what was left; a second Ctrl+C leaves at once.
- **Signals.** SIGTERM (`kill`, a logout), SIGHUP (the terminal or SSH session closed) and SIGINT
  stop the app the same way, in a window and in a terminal: the jobs stop and remove their test
  data, then the app exits with code 130. A second signal leaves at once.
- **Run files**: open a `.oprobe`, `.prove.json`, report `.json` or `op.toml` file with File ▸ Open Run File… (the
  system's open dialog, filtered to those types), drop it on the window (the window is outlined
  while a file is dragged over it), or double-click a `.oprobe` / `.json` file: `oprobe.app` (macOS), the `.msi`
  (Windows) and the Linux desktop archive's `.desktop` entry and MIME type
  (`application/x-oprobe-run`) register `.oprobe` files, and run `oprobe FILE`, which opens the
  file in the app. The archives and the `.deb` / `.rpm` register nothing.
- **Progress**: a running job shows its progress on the Dock or taskbar icon. When it ends while
  the window is in the background, a notification says so and the Dock icon or taskbar button
  asks for attention.
- **Accessibility**: messages in the notice bar are read out by screen readers; control heights
  grow with the system's text size; the dialogs appear without a fade when reduced motion is on.

**Profile.** One run, from the verdict down to the raw numbers:

- **The numbers**: goodput, bandwidth, p50 / p99 / p99.9, failed operations (per operation) and
  throttled requests (per request), with how many operations and requests were measured.
  A **Read these numbers with care** note comes first when the client was saturated, the run is
  partial, open-loop arrivals started late, or too few operations were measured.
- **Findings**, each with its remedy and the evidence it rests on (below). Its named values are
  labelled in the app's language and formatted like the tiles (`9.87 ms`, `2.60 %`). **Show N
  examples** expands the waterfalls of the operations that show the problem.
- **Where the time went**: the stage split of every operation, and of each verb with its
  operations per second, MiB/s, requests per operation and, when any, its throttled share.
- **Requests by API**: for each S3 API, the request count, the status codes, TTFB p50 / p99,
  total p50 / p99 (the same statistics as `oprobe show`) with a bar of the p50 inside the p99,
  scaled to the slowest API, bytes down / up and connection reuse. For a run that wrote in
  parts, a **Writes** line gives the multipart part size OpenDAL used (with the requested chunk
  and the service's limits when it was clamped) and the parts uploaded with their mean size.
  Click an API to list its slowest requests, and one of those to see its operation's
  waterfall.
- **Retries and failures**: retries, time spent waiting between attempts, 429 / 503 responses,
  the longest `Retry-After`, other errors and failure classes.
- **The slowest operations** as a request waterfall. Each request is on a shared time axis and
  coloured by stage, the body's wait for the consumer (stall) its own segment; the wait before a
  retry is drawn as a line in the retry colour. Hovering or focusing a request reads out its stages and,
  when recorded, the provider's error code (`SlowDown`), `Retry-After`, tail-cut / incomplete body status, the connection's rtt,
  min rtt and retransmits, `Server-Timing`, HTTP/2 active
  streams, when the upload reached the kernel and was acknowledged, the CDN cache status, the
  region and the request ID ([request signals](reading-the-profile.md#request-signals)). An operation whose
  async call stack was captured has **Async call stack while in flight** under it, closed until
  clicked.
- **Timeline**, with a verb filter above it (All verbs, or one verb):
  - goodput (successful operations) with the attempted rate, failures included, as a faint line
    behind it, and the intervals with throttled responses or failed operations shaded;
  - p50 / p99 / p99.9; an interval with too few operations for a quantile (fewer than
    10 / (1 − q): 1 000 for p99) draws it faint and dashed, and the readout says so
    (`n=12, too few for p99`);
  - throughput: MiB per second read and written, interval by interval (the bandwidth tile over
    time);
  - requests per second (retries included);
  - **Problems per second**, on its own axis and only when any happened: the retries, the
    throttled responses and the failed operations per second (on the requests' axis a few
    retries would be flat at zero; here one 429 does not look like a thousand either);
  - the number of requests in flight, with the connections dialed in each interval (churn
    behind a latency spike) and, faint, the client's CPU in cores busy (its saturation over
    time).

  Throughput, requests, problems and in-flight are not split by verb: with a verb chosen they
  say "all verbs". Every chart ends where the measured window ends, as the tiles do: what
  operations did while draining after the window counts in its last interval. A legend lists
  only the series that are not zero throughout.
- **Latency distribution**: a tail plot, the share of operations slower than each latency on
  log axes (latency across, 100 % down to 0.01 % up the side), with p50, p99 and p99.9 marked,
  so the tail gets as much room as the body. It is drawn from every row when no row was sampled
  away, else from the run's latency histogram, which counts every operation. With a verb chosen
  (and no range), it is that verb's.
- **Heatmap**: operations by start time and latency, in fine rows (1-1.5-2-3-5-7 per decade, the
  slowest row closed at the next step) when every row was kept, with a colour key from the fewest to the most operations in a cell. Click a cell to list its slowest
  operations (verb, key, latency, status, attempts), and one of those to see its waterfall.
- **Connections**: the connections dialed, each count with its window (`28 during warm-up · 1
  in the window`), failed dials, reuse, the protocols used, TLS, the proxy, peak requests in
  flight, each dial phase's p50 / p99 (DNS, TCP, proxy CONNECT, TLS), and whether the network or
  the server is the limit: the kernel's minimum round trip (the network's) and its smoothed
  round trip p50 / p99 — on a fast network the smoothed one includes the server's delay and
  delayed acknowledgements, and the app says so when it is far above the minimum —, the
  connections that retransmitted, the share of sending time limited by the receive window or
  the send buffer, the delivery rate, the TLS handshakes (resumed share, HelloRetryRequests)
  and the cold start (the warm-up dials' connect time and the first operations' latency).
- **Details** (open on demand):
  - bytes asked for against bytes moved: read, write and request amplification, cache hits,
    and the bytes on the wire (in / out, from the kernel's counters) when they were measured;
  - the hottest keys, object sizes (as ranges: `0 B`, `4 KiB – 64 KiB`, …), prefixes, the first
    read and re-reads of a key, and server addresses, each with its share of the requests (with
    a bar), its throttled share, error share and p99 (a column no row has is left out: hot keys
    carry their share of the throttling only).
- **Run setup** (open on demand): target, workload, load, dataset, mix, the write path, seed, the client (CPU and
  scheduling lag), the share of trace rows kept, and the `oprobe run …` command that runs it
  again.

**A time range.** The timeline charts and the heatmap share one time cursor: hovering one shows
the time on all. Drag across any of them to select a range, shaded on every time chart. The key
numbers, the requests by API, the verbs, the distribution and the slowest operations then show
that range, recomputed from the trace rows (an operation counts in the range it started in, a
request in the range it was sent in); when the run kept only a share of its rows, the range says
so and weights each row by the operations it stands for. Escape, a double-click on a chart or
**Clear** drops the range. `oprobe show RUN --since 3s --until 8s` prints the same range.

Every chart has the Image role and a label that summarises it for screen readers.

Each finding carries the evidence it rests on:

| Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|
| `throttling` | the share throttled at each number of requests in flight, with the fitted limit's interval shaded |
| `key_limit`, `repeated_reads` | the hottest keys as horizontal bars of their share of all throttling (of all requests when nothing was throttled) |
| `small_ranges` | bytes asked for against bytes downloaded, and requests per operation |
| `rate_limit` | throttled responses per second |
| `bandwidth_cap` | bandwidth (MiB/s) over the run |
| `tail_stragglers`, `hung_requests` | the latency tail plot, with p50, p99 and p99.9 marked |
| `errors` | failed operations per second |

**Operator.** The run's layer stack beside each finding's remedy. A finding's **Prove** (and
**Prove this remedy** in Profile) proves that finding as its `next` command (`oprobe prove RUN CODE`, with its objective) does: prove
sizes the remedy from the run (a limit from the fitted throttling limit, say) and then proves
it. Toggle a layer or change a value (a limit, a chunk size) yourself and **Prove** proves your
change with the values you set. The trials stream in live and their A/B pairs are drawn as they
converge: each pair's change as a dot, the running estimate with its 95 % interval narrowing,
and the noise floor around no change, until the sequential test decides: **improved**,
**worse** or **inconclusive**. **Copy** puts the winning diff (Rust or TOML) on the clipboard; when
the run came from an `op.toml` file, **Save to op.toml** writes the proven change back to it in
place (preserving credentials and `${ENV}` references).

**Compare.** Two runs, or the operators of one multi-operator run, side by side: goodput,
bandwidth, requests per second, latency p50 / p99 / p99.9, failed operations, retries, throttled
responses, the stage split and the findings of each, with their goodput, p99 and requests per
second over time and their latency tails drawn on one chart each, and each backend API's
requests and TTFB p99 in every run. Shares (errors, throttled) change by percentage
points. The changes are shown in a neutral colour, never as better or worse: each column is a
single run, and its difference includes run-to-run noise. To measure a change, prove it.

## Language

The app speaks **简体中文** and **English**. It follows the system locale (a `zh` locale selects
Chinese) and a setting in the app overrides it. The CLI, the JSON output and the run files are
English only.

## Keys

`mod` is ⌘ on macOS and Ctrl elsewhere (and in a terminal).

| Keys | Does |
|---|---|
| mod+N | New Run… |
| mod+O | Open Run File… |
| mod+R | Run the selected run again |
| mod+. | Stop the running job |
| mod+shift+P | Prove (your change, else the chosen or top finding's remedy) |
| mod+1, mod+2 | Profile, Operator |
| ctrl+⌘+S (macOS), mod+shift+S | Show or hide the sidebar |
| mod+shift+C | Copy the selected run IDs |
| ⌘⌫ (macOS), Delete | Delete the selected runs (asks first; Undo brings them back) |
| ↑ ↓, Shift+↑ ↓, Home, End, letters | Move, extend and find in the sidebar's list |
| mod+, | Settings |
| F11 (Windows, Linux), ctrl+⌘+F (macOS) | Full screen |
| Ctrl+Q (Linux), ⌘Q (macOS) | Quit (asks first while a job runs) |
| F10 (terminal) | The main menu |
| Ctrl+C (terminal) | Quit (stops a job and cleans up first) |

## Without a display

Over SSH or in a container the app opens in the terminal. Where neither works (no terminal, a
pipe), use the CLI: `oprobe run`, `oprobe show`, `oprobe prove` print the same profile as text or
JSON.


<!-- source: docs/install.md -->

# Installing oprobe

## Quick

| Platform | Command |
|---|---|
| macOS, Linux | `curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh \| sh` |
| macOS, Linux (CLI only) | `curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh \| sh -s -- --cli` |
| Windows | `irm https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 \| iex`, or the `.msi` |
| Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL | the `.deb` / `.rpm` from the release page |
| Rust ≥ 1.97 (from source) | `cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe --tag v9.3.3 oprobe` |

Then try it with no account: `oprobe demo` ([getting started](getting-started.md)).

## The app and the CLI-only build

Every platform has two builds of the same program:

- **the app build** (the default everywhere): the four commands plus the app, in a native window
  on macOS and Windows and in the terminal everywhere ([app](app.md));
- **the CLI-only build** (`oprobe-cli-<ver>-<target>` archives, `install.sh --cli`,
  `install.ps1 -Cli`, `cargo install … --no-default-features --features cli`): the four
  commands, text and JSON, no app. It is smaller and pulls in no UI toolkit, for servers, CI and
  containers.

Both include the common cloud services (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, OSS, COS, OBS, B2, WebDAV) plus
`fs`, `memory` and the lab. `--features all-services` adds the rest.

## The install scripts

`install.sh` (Linux, macOS) and `install.ps1` (Windows) download the archive for your platform,
verify it against `SHA256SUMS`, verify its build provenance when they can
([verifying](#verifying-a-download)) and install `oprobe` (Linux and macOS: `~/.local/bin`;
Windows: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\oprobe`). `sh install.sh --help` and
`Get-Help ./install.ps1` print every option.

| Option | Variable | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `--cli` / `-Cli` | `OPROBE_FLAVOR=cli` | install the CLI-only build |
| `--version X.Y.Z` / `-Version` | `OPROBE_VERSION` | install this version instead of the latest |
| `--dir DIR` / `-InstallDir` | `OPROBE_INSTALL_DIR` | install somewhere else |
| `--no-modify-path` | `OPROBE_MODIFY_PATH=0` | never touch `PATH` (`=1`: add it without asking) |
| | `OPROBE_RELEASE_BASE=URL` | release download base (mirrors, tests; default `https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases`) |
| | `OPROBE_VERIFY=auto\|require\|checksum` | after the checksum: verify the provenance when this machine can (default), insist on it, or skip it |

They find the latest version without the rate-limited GitHub API when they can: the release's
`latest.json`, then the `releases/latest` redirect, then the API.

**PATH.** When the install directory is not on `PATH`, `install.sh` offers to append it to your
shell's rc file (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.bashrc` or `~/.bash_profile` on macOS,
`~/.config/fish/config.fish`, else `~/.profile`). Piped from `curl`, it asks on the terminal when
there is one; without a terminal (CI, `docker build`) it changes nothing and prints the line to
add. `install.ps1` adds its directory to the user `PATH` and to the current session. It installs
the native ARM64 build on ARM64 Windows.

**Updating.** Run the install script again, install the newer package, or run `cargo install`
with the newer tag.

## Release assets

| Asset | Platform |
|---|---|
| `oprobe-<ver>-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` / `aarch64-…-musl` | Linux, static (any distribution); the app in the terminal |
| `oprobe-<ver>-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` / `aarch64-…-gnu` | Linux, glibc ≥ 2.35 |
| `oprobe_<ver>-1_amd64.deb` / `_arm64.deb` | Debian, Ubuntu |
| `oprobe-<ver>-1.x86_64.rpm` / `.aarch64.rpm` | Fedora, RHEL, SUSE |
| `oprobe-desktop-<ver>-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` | Linux with the window (GTK 4.14+; `install.sh`, `.desktop` entry, icon) |
| `oprobe-<ver>-universal-apple-darwin.tar.gz` | macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) |
| `oprobe-<ver>-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` / `x86_64-apple-darwin` | macOS, one architecture |
| `oprobe-<ver>-macos-universal.pkg` | macOS installer: `/usr/local/bin/oprobe` |
| `oprobe-<ver>-macos-universal.dmg` | macOS app: `oprobe.app` (the same binary as the `.pkg`) |
| `oprobe-<ver>-x64.msi` / `-arm64.msi` | Windows installer: `PATH`, Start menu entry, removable in *Apps* |
| `oprobe-<ver>-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` / `aarch64-…` | Windows portable |
| `oprobe-cli-<ver>-<target>.tar.gz` / `.zip` | the CLI-only build for each target above (`universal-apple-darwin` on macOS) |
| `latest.json` | machine-readable index: version, every asset's URL, size and SHA-256 |
| `install.sh` / `install.ps1` | the install scripts |
| `SHA256SUMS` | checksums of every asset |

Archives contain `oprobe` (`oprobe.exe`), `README.md`, `LICENSE` and `CHANGELOG.md`.

## Windows

```powershell
irm https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex   # no admin rights
& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.ps1))) -Cli
```

The `.msi` installs for all users (Start menu entry, `PATH`, removable in *Apps*).

## Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora

```bash
sudo apt install ./oprobe_<ver>-1_amd64.deb
sudo dnf install ./oprobe-<ver>-1.x86_64.rpm
```

## From source

```bash
cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe --tag v9.3.3 oprobe                                         # the app in the terminal
cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe --tag v9.3.3 oprobe --features gui                          # plus native windows (Linux: libgtk-4-dev)
cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe --tag v9.3.3 oprobe --no-default-features --features cli    # the CLI only
```

oprobe is not on crates.io. To embed oprobe's instrumentation in your own program use
[`oprobe-trace`](embedding.md).

## Verifying a download

The install scripts always check the SHA-256 and, when the GitHub CLI is installed and logged in,
the build provenance. A check that runs and fails stops the install; a check that cannot run is a
warning, or an error with `OPROBE_VERIFY=require`.

**Checksum.** Detects corrupted or truncated downloads. `SHA256SUMS` comes from the same release
as the archive, so it proves the download is intact, not who built it.

```bash
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS                    # Linux
shasum -a 256 --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS                # macOS
Get-FileHash oprobe-9.3.2-x64.msi -Algorithm SHA256          # Windows
```

**Build provenance.** Every asset has a [SLSA build provenance](https://slsa.dev/) attestation
signed by GitHub Actions, which proves it was built by this repository's release workflow from a
given commit:

```bash
gh attestation verify oprobe-9.3.2-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz --repo hxddh/oprobe \
  --signer-workflow hxddh/oprobe/.github/workflows/release.yml
```

**minisign.** The release workflow can also sign `SHA256SUMS` with minisign
(`SHA256SUMS.minisig`) and embed the public key in the install scripts, which then verify the
signature when `gh` is not available. This happens only for releases made with a signing key
configured; a release without `SHA256SUMS.minisig` is not signed, and its install scripts check
no signature. The release notes say which applies.

These say who built a file; they are not operating-system code signing (below).

## First open of unsigned packages

The project has no Apple or Microsoft code-signing certificate, so the `.pkg`, `.dmg` and `.msi`
are **not signed or notarized**. The operating system asks for one confirmation the first time:

- **macOS 15 (Sequoia) and later**: open `oprobe.app` (or the `.pkg`) once and close the warning;
  then open *System Settings → Privacy & Security*, scroll to the message about oprobe, click
  **Open Anyway** and confirm with your password.
- **macOS 14 and earlier**: right-click `oprobe.app` → *Open* → *Open*.
- **Either, from a terminal**: `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/oprobe.app`.
- **Windows**: SmartScreen says "Windows protected your PC": click **More info** → **Run anyway**.

The install scripts, `cargo install` and the plain archives used from a terminal are not affected.
The app is signed ad hoc, so macOS may refuse to verify its developer, but never reports it as
damaged. Verify the download ([above](#verifying-a-download)) before you
confirm.


<!-- source: docs/troubleshooting.md -->

# Troubleshooting

`oprobe run` checks the operator before it measures (a preflight: credentials, the network path,
list and write permission on the prefix). When something is wrong it stops with an error that
carries a stable code (`-o json`: `error.code`, plus `error.docs` linking to this page) and usually
a `hint:` line. `--dry-run` shows the plan without sending a request.

## Common problems

| Code / symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `usage.unknown_target` | the `OPERATOR` is neither a URL, an `op.toml` file nor a configured name | pass a URL (`s3://bucket/prefix`), a file, or define `[operators.NAME]` in the config file |
| `usage.unknown_run` | no run matches the reference | `oprobe show --list`; use more characters of the id |
| `config.invalid`, `config.unknown_option` | a typo in `op.toml` or the config file, or an option the service does not know | the error names the key and the closest valid one ([op.toml](operator.md)) |
| `auth.no_credentials`, `auth.denied`, `AccessDenied`, `SignatureDoesNotMatch` | missing or wrong credentials | export `AWS_*` / `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` / `AZURE_STORAGE_*`, or set them in `[options]`; oprobe needs list/read/write/delete on the prefix, or measure read-only with `--existing PREFIX` |
| `net.tls`, `invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer` | a private CA or a TLS-inspecting proxy | `http.ca_cert = "corp.pem"` in `op.toml` (or `--set http.ca_cert=corp.pem`); `http.insecure = true` for development endpoints only |
| `net.dns`, `no addresses` | a wrong endpoint, or a network where only the proxy resolves names | check `options.endpoint`; set `HTTPS_PROXY` |
| `net.unreachable`, `connection refused` | nothing listening | check the endpoint and port; is MinIO or `oprobe lab` running? |
| `RequestTimeTooSkewed` | the local clock is off by more than 15 minutes | enable NTP |
| `PermanentRedirect`, `AuthorizationHeaderMalformed`, `region is missing` | wrong region | `--set options.region=…` or `AWS_REGION`; R2 uses `auto` |
| `safety.read_only` (exit 5) | a write under `--read-only` / `--existing` | drop the flag, or profile existing objects with `--existing PREFIX` |
| `safety.budget_exceeded` (exit 4) | a budget stopped the run | raise `--max-*`; the partial run is saved |
| exit 3 after `prove` | the change is worse on the objective | read the evidence; try another value with `--with` |

## Situations

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| leftover `oprobe-run-*` prefixes | a run was killed hard (a second Ctrl-C, OOM, power loss): the next run against the same target deletes them (it says so), except under `--read-only`; or delete the prefix with your usual tools |
| `client_bound` on a remote store | the profiling process is the bottleneck (CPU, tiny objects); the profile's `self` section says why. Larger objects or fewer workers |
| `client_bound`: "cannot tell too few workers from a service at its capacity" | an open loop (`--rate`) fell behind with every worker busy: a steady overload shows one level of requests in flight. Vary the load (`--set shape=ramp:FROM..TO/D`): a service that queues is then `throttling`, one with room leaves the workers as the bound |
| "N of M scheduled arrivals never completed" and a Critical verdict | the open loop stalled: more than 1 % of its arrivals never completed, so its p99 has no upper bound. Lower `--rate`, or see the finding beside it for who fell behind |
| `oprobe` asks nothing in a script | it never prompts: pass an operator, and use `--non-interactive` to rule out redraws |
| `cannot open a window` | no display (SSH, a server): the app opens in the terminal; Linux packages built with `--features gui` need GTK 4 |
| `oprobe show FILE` fails on a file from `oprobe-trace` | the file is from a newer major version, or was cut short; write it again with `Handle::save` |
| macOS "cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified" / Windows SmartScreen | the packages are unsigned: [first open](install.md#first-open-of-unsigned-packages) |

## Error codes

Every error carries one of these codes. The exit code follows the class: `2` usage/config, `1`
runtime, `3` the proven change is worse, `4` budget, `5` safety refusal, `130` interrupted.

<a id="usage-invalid_argument"></a>
### `usage.invalid_argument` (exit 2)

A flag or argument is malformed: an unknown flag, a value that does not parse
(`--max-bytes lots`), an unknown `--set` path, or an address `oprobe lab --bind` cannot listen
on (the port is taken: `--bind 127.0.0.1:0` takes a free one). With `-o json` argument errors
are JSON too. Fix the argument; `--help` lists what the command accepts.

<a id="usage-unknown_target"></a>
### `usage.unknown_target` (exit 2)

The `OPERATOR` is neither a URL, an existing `op.toml` file nor a name under `[operators.NAME]`
in the config file, or no operator was given. The hint lists the configured names.

<a id="usage-unknown_run"></a>
### `usage.unknown_run` (exit 2)

No stored run matches the reference. `oprobe show --list`; use more characters of the id,
`last`, `last~N`, or a path to a `.oprobe` file.

<a id="usage-unknown_baseline"></a>
### `usage.unknown_baseline` (exit 2)

A 5.x baseline name was given. oprobe 6 has no baselines: compare runs in the app, or prove a
change with `oprobe prove`.

<a id="config-invalid"></a>
### `config.invalid` (exit 2)

An operator file or the config file does not parse, or has an invalid value (an unknown key, a
size that does not parse). The message names the key.

"`op.toml` now names …, not the operator the run used": `prove` replays a stored run with the
secrets of the operator it was run with, and the operator file or configured operator it names
now has another URL or endpoint. Its keys are not sent to the run's endpoint. Put the file back
as the run had it, or start a new run with the operator you mean.

<a id="config-unknown_option"></a>
### `config.unknown_option` (exit 2)

A service option the OpenDAL service does not know (`[options]`, `--set options.KEY=…`). The
message names the closest valid option.

<a id="auth-no_credentials"></a>
### `auth.no_credentials` (exit 1)

No credentials were found. Export the provider's variables (`AWS_*`,
`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, `AZURE_STORAGE_*`) or set them in `[options]` (values may
reference `${ENV_VARS}`).

<a id="auth-denied"></a>
### `auth.denied` (exit 1)

The service refused the credentials or the operation (`AccessDenied`, `SignatureDoesNotMatch`,
403). oprobe needs list/read/write/delete on the prefix; profile read-only with
`--existing PREFIX`.

<a id="net-unreachable"></a>
### `net.unreachable` (exit 1, retryable)

Nothing answered (`connection refused`, reset, no route). Check the endpoint and port; is MinIO or
`oprobe lab` running? When the requests go through a proxy (`http.proxy`, or `HTTPS_PROXY` /
`HTTP_PROXY` / `ALL_PROXY` unless `NO_PROXY` exempts the endpoint), the proxy is what the client
connects to, and the message names it ("connection refused by the proxy 127.0.0.1:3128"): check
that it is running, or connect directly with `--set http.proxy=none`.

<a id="net-dns"></a>
### `net.dns` (exit 1, retryable)

The endpoint's name did not resolve. Check `options.endpoint`; on networks where only the proxy
resolves names set `HTTPS_PROXY`.

<a id="net-tls"></a>
### `net.tls` (exit 1)

The TLS handshake failed (`invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer`, an expired or mismatched
certificate): a private CA or a TLS-inspecting proxy. Set `http.ca_cert` (or `SSL_CERT_FILE`);
`http.insecure = true` for development endpoints only.

<a id="net-timeout"></a>
### `net.timeout` (exit 1, retryable)

A request or connection timed out. Check the network path; lower the concurrency if the client or
the link is saturated. A timeout inside a run is a finding (`hung_requests`), not an error.

<a id="net-rate_limited"></a>
### `net.rate_limited` (exit 1, retryable)

An HTTP API other than the storage operator refused the request because its rate limit is
exhausted (429, or 403 with no quota left). Wait and retry. Your storage credentials are not
involved.

<a id="net-http"></a>
### `net.http` (exit 1)

An HTTP API other than the storage operator answered with an error. The message names the URL and
the status. Your storage credentials are not involved.

<a id="storage-not_found"></a>
### `storage.not_found` (exit 1)

The bucket, container, root or `--existing` prefix does not exist, or holds no objects. Check the
URL and region; with `--existing PREFIX` list the prefix first.

<a id="storage-throttled"></a>
### `storage.throttled` (exit 1, retryable)

The service rate-limited the preflight itself (429, 503 SlowDown). Inside a run, throttling is a
finding (`throttling`) and never fails the run: `oprobe prove RUN throttling` sizes the
`ConcurrentLimitLayer` that avoids it.

<a id="storage-unsupported"></a>
### `storage.unsupported` (exit 1)

The service does not support an operation the workload needs (multipart, list). Pick another
preset.

<a id="safety-budget_exceeded"></a>
### `safety.budget_exceeded` (exit 4)

A budget (`--max-requests`, `--max-bytes`, `--max-duration`, or `[defaults.budgets]`) stopped the
command. Budgets cover the whole command: every operator of `run`, every trial of `prove`, and
every HTTP request sent to the target before cleanup (the preflight, the dataset upload and
retries included; for `fs://` and `memory://`, every call of the service). The request the budget had no room for was not sent, the operations in flight
were cut, their multipart uploads aborted, the partial run saved and the test data cleaned up.
When the budget runs out during the preflight or the dataset upload there is no run to save (and
nothing is left on the target: the preflight's probe object is deleted outside the budget).
"the next request (8.0 MiB) does not fit the byte budget: 1 B of 4.0 MiB used" means
`--max-bytes` is smaller than one request body (a multipart part, an object): raise it above
that size. "the dataset alone (…) does not fit the byte budget" means the objects to upload are
larger than `--max-bytes`: nothing was uploaded. Lower `--objects` or `--object-size`, or raise
the budget. Raise the budget or shorten the run; `--dry-run` shows the estimates.

<a id="safety-read_only"></a>
### `safety.read_only` (exit 5)

The command would write or delete under `--read-only` / `--existing`. Drop the flag, or profile
existing objects with `--existing PREFIX`.

<a id="safety-refused"></a>
### `safety.refused` (exit 5)

A safety rail refused the command, for example deleting a run that is still being written, or a
lab limit.

<a id="run-sla_failed"></a>
### `run.sla_failed` (exit 3)

A 5.x SLA check failed. oprobe 6 has no SLA: it reports failures as findings, and `--set sla…`
is refused. Exit 3 now means that `prove` found the change worse on the objective.

<a id="run-regression"></a>
### `run.regression` (exit 3)

The change made things worse on the objective: `prove`'s verdict is `worse`. Read the evidence
(the trials and the secondary metrics); try another value with `--with`.

<a id="run-interrupted"></a>
### `run.interrupted` (exit 130, retryable)

Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, SIGHUP, a closed stderr (the terminal or SSH session went away, or
`2>&1 | head` read enough) or Stop ended the command, at any point: while it opened the target,
uploaded its dataset or measured. The requests in flight were cut, the multipart uploads they
belonged to aborted, and the test data cleaned up, unless a second signal ended the cleanup too.
A run that was measuring is saved as a partial run. Run it again.

"N multipart uploads could not be aborted and may still hold parts (…)" in the message or in the
cleanup error names uploads the stop could not remove: an abort the service refused or did not
answer within 30 s, an upload whose creation did not answer within 10 s of the stop, or one
still in flight 45 s after it. Their parts are billed until the upload is aborted: list and abort
them with the service's tools (`aws s3api list-multipart-uploads` / `abort-multipart-upload`).

<a id="internal"></a>
### `internal` (exit 1)

An unexpected failure. Rerun with the same arguments; if it persists, report it with the command
line and the error message.

[Reading the profile](reading-the-profile.md) explains each verdict and section.


<!-- source: docs/privacy.md -->

# Privacy

**oprobe sends no telemetry.** No usage statistics, crash reports or analytics, and no setting to
turn any on. Neither does `oprobe-trace`.

## What oprobe connects to

| When | Where |
|---|---|
| `run`, `prove`, the app | the storage endpoint of the operator you give it (and your proxy, if `HTTPS_PROXY` or `http.proxy` is set); that cloud's credential providers (instance metadata, STS, SSO) when the credential chain needs them |
| `demo`, `lab`, `lab://…` operators | nothing: the lab runs inside oprobe on 127.0.0.1 |
| `show`, `show --list`, `show --rm` | nothing |

Nothing else. oprobe never checks for updates by itself; the install scripts talk to GitHub when
you run them.

## What oprobe stores

- **Runs** in `<data dir>/oprobe/runs/` (or `$OPROBE_DATA_DIR`): the report, the operator spec,
  the workload and one row per operation and request. Object keys, request IDs and remote IP
  addresses are part of a run. Secrets are not: credential options (`secret_access_key`,
  `account_key`, `sas_token`, `password`, `*_key`, …) are redacted before anything is printed or
  saved. Every text loses the credentials it carries, in an operator, an option, a proxy
  setting or the text of an error ([what is removed](#what-is-removed-from-a-text)). Errors,
  warnings and log events are printed the same way.
- **The host** is recorded as OS, architecture, CPU count and a hash of the host name, never the
  name itself.
- **Pending-cleanup markers** in `<data dir>/oprobe/pending/`: while a run that writes is going,
  one small file names its target and its `oprobe-run-*` prefix. It is removed once the test data
  is deleted; one left by a killed run tells the next run against that target what to delete.
- **The config file** holds what you put there.

Delete runs with `oprobe show --rm RUN…`, or remove the data directory.

## What is removed from a text

One function redacts every text before it is recorded, stored or printed
(`oprobe_trace::util::strip_url_credentials`). It removes:

- **`user:password@`** of every URL, also when the password holds a `/`, `?` or `#` (an AWS
  secret key typed into a URL unescaped).
- **Secret parameters**, by name and whatever their case: `*signature*` (`X-Amz-Signature`,
  `X-Goog-Signature`, `x-oss-signature`, `q-signature`), `sig` and `*_sig` (an Azure SAS, a
  Swift `temp_url_sig`), `*token*`, `*credential*`, access key ids (`AWSAccessKeyId`, …),
  `upload_id` (the session of a GCS resumable upload is a bearer credential), `*secret*`,
  `*password*`, `*session*`, `*authorization*`, `*jwt*`, `*hmac*`, `key`, `*_key`, `apikey`.
  They are removed from a URL's query, from its fragment (`#access_token=…`), from a query
  with no URL around it (`GET /b/k?X-Amz-Signature=…`), from a bare parameter list (an SAS
  token `sv=…&sig=…`) and from a percent-encoded URL passed as a value
  (`?next=https%3A%2F%2F…%3Fsig%3D…`). The other parameters stay, in order.
- **The value of a lone `name=value`** with such a name (the `Signature=…` and `Credential=…`
  of a quoted `Authorization` header, `password=…`): it reads `name=<redacted>`.
- **The value of an `Authorization` header** quoted in a text (`Authorization: Bearer …`).

What only describes a request stays readable: `X-Amz-Expires`, `X-Amz-Date`, an SAS's `se` and
`sp`; the cursors and key ranges of a listing (`continuation-token`, `pageToken`, `start_key`,
`end_key`, `partition-key`, `marker`), which name a position and grant nothing; S3's `uploadId`;
switches such as `skip_signature=true`; an environment reference (`${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}`);
and a bare `key=…` outside a parameter list, which names an object. A name that only looks
like a secret's is redacted.

What it cannot know: a credential in none of these forms (a bare token in a path or a
sentence, a JSON field), and a password before whose first `/` stands only a port number
(`user:8080/…@host` reads as `host:port/path`). Percent-encode a password you put in a URL, or
better, give credentials as options or through the environment.

## `.oprobe` files from `oprobe-trace`

`Handle::save` writes what the layer saw in your process: the aggregates and a sample of
operations and their requests, with their API, method, status, timing, bytes, connection and
request ID. Object keys are never stored: an operation's key is its first path segment (at most
32 bytes) and a hash of the whole key (`logs/#3f2a…`), so a top-level directory name can be in
the file, but not a key. Request IDs and remote addresses are. Credentials never are: the
text of a failed request or operation loses the credentials it carries
([what is removed](#what-is-removed-from-a-text): the signature and token of a presigned or SAS
URL included, with or without a URL around them) when it is recorded, so neither an
`Exporter`, a `Snapshot` nor a file ever holds them. Review a file before you attach it to an
issue.

## Test data in your bucket

`oprobe run` writes under `<prefix>/oprobe-run-<id>/` and deletes it at the end, verifying the
prefix is empty. `--read-only` and `--existing` never write; `--dry-run` sends nothing. A run
killed hard (a second Ctrl-C, OOM, power loss) can leave its prefix behind; delete it with your
usual tools.
